value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Chemical Engineering is committed to providing academic advising in support of doctoral student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The department’s graduate handbook provides information and suggested timelines for advising meetings in the different stages of the doctoral program. PhD students are initially assigned a program advisor at the outset of their enrollment at Stanford. This faculty member will provide initial guidance in course selection, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and identifying doctoral research opportunities. The department requires formal lab rotations for two quarters before selecting a doctoral research/thesis advisor. Graduate students are expected to select a thesis advisor before the end of the first year of the program. Students are encouraged to collaborate with their advisor to establish a dissertation project and form a Dissertation Reading Committee. Advancement to doctoral candidacy is expected to occur before the end of the fourth quarter of the program. The process and timing of advisor selection are described in the Graduate Academic Policies and Procedures (GAP) . The research supervisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor, and will ultimately direct the student’s dissertation. Most students find an advisor from our department’s primary faculty members. However, the research advisor may be a faculty member from another Stanford department familiar with supervising doctoral students and can provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program. When the research advisor is from outside our department, the student will also identify a program advisor from our primary faculty to guide departmental requirements and opportunities. Thesis advisors are expected to meet with graduate students at least once yearly to discuss and help develop the student’s program plan. Additionally, advisors and students should meet regularly throughout the year to discuss the student’s professional development in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) meets with all doctoral students at the start of the first year and is available by email and during office hours during the academic year. Our department’s student services office is also an essential part of the doctoral advising team: they inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and they maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. Students are encouraged to talk with the DGS and the student services office as they consider advisor selection or for guidance in working with their advisor(s). Our doctoral students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. Additionally, the program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE) and in the Graduate Academic Policies (GAP).

value.A3i6E: ICME is a degree-granting (MS/PhD) interdisciplinary institute at the intersection of mathematics, computing, engineering, and applied sciences. ICME was founded in 2004, building upon the Scientific Computing and Computational Mathematics Program (est. 1989). At ICME, we design state-of-the-art mathematical and computational models, methods, and algorithms for engineering and science applications. The program collaborates closely with engineers and scientists in academia and industry to develop improved computational approaches and advance disciplinary fields. In particular, it leverages Stanford’s strength in engineering applications in the physical, biological, mathematical, and information sciences and has established connections with nearly 20 departments across five schools at Stanford. The program identifies research areas that would benefit from a multidisciplinary approach in which computational mathematics is critical. This multidisciplinary intellectual environment is a core strength of ICME, with interaction among students and faculty with diverse backgrounds and expertise. Students and faculty are active in many research areas: aerodynamics and space applications, fluid dynamics, protein folding, data science, including machine learning and recommender systems, ocean dynamics, climate modeling, reservoir engineering, computer graphics, financial mathematics, and many more. The program trains students and scholars from across Stanford in mathematical modeling, scientific computing, and advanced computational algorithms at the undergraduate and graduate levels. Courses typically provide strong theoretical foundations for solving real-world problems and numerical computations to facilitate the application of mathematical techniques and theories. Training offered includes matrix computations, computational probability and combinatorial optimization, optimization, stochastics, numerical solution of partial differential equations, parallel computer algorithms, and new computing paradigms. ICME offers service courses for undergraduates and graduate students to fulfill departmental requirements, core courses for master’s and doctoral students in Computational and Mathematical Engineering, and specialized electives in various application areas. The ICME master’s program offers a general Computational and Mathematical Engineering track as well as three specialized tracks: Data Science, Imaging Science, and Mathematical and Computational Finance. Prerequisites Fundamental courses in mathematics and computing may be needed as prerequisites for other courses in the program. Check the prerequisites of each required course. Recommended preparatory courses include advanced undergraduate-level courses in linear algebra, probability, differential equations, stochastics, and numerical methods and proficiency in programming. Financial Assistance The department awards a limited number of fellowships, course assistantships, and research assistantships to incoming graduate students. Most course and research assistantships are awarded to students in the doctoral program in ICME. If there are insufficient PhD students to staff all course and research assistantships, these positions may be open to master’s students. However, master’s students are not guaranteed financial assistance.

value.A3i6E: Doctor of Philosophy in Computer Science The PhD degree is intended primarily for students who desire a career in research, advanced development, or teaching. For this type of work, a broad background in computer science and the engineering sciences, and intensive study and research experience in a specialized area are the necessary requisites. The degree of Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) is conferred on candidates who have demonstrated to the satisfaction of our department: High attainment in a particular field of knowledge. Ability to do independent investigation and present the results of research. They must satisfy the general requirements for advanced degrees, the program requirements specified, and the doctoral requirements for candidacy, as outlined in our department. Guidelines for Reasonable Progress By the end of the first academic year, you should align with a permanent advisor. Students are welcome to switch advisors; however, a student should not have significant periods of time (after the first year) with no advisor. A student must make satisfactory progress in their research, as determined by their advisor. Participation in research throughout the student's career routinely satisfies the research requirement. Three foundation/breadth requirements must be completed by spring quarter of the second year. A student should meet the eligibility requirements and file for Candidacy by the end of the second year in their program. All courses must be completed by the end of the third year. Any deviation from this timeline must be approved in advance by both the student advisor and the director of the PhD program. By spring quarter of the third year, a student should pass a Qualifying Examination in the area of their intended dissertation. Within one year of passing the Qualifying Examination, a student should form a reading committee and submit a signed Reading Committee form to the PhD Student Services Office at phdstudentservices@cs.stanford.edu . By spring quarter of the fourth year, a student should schedule the Thesis Proposal with the reading committee members and submit the Thesis Proposal form to the PhD Student Services Office at phdstudentservices@cs.stanford.edu . The Teaching Requirement must be completed by their fourth year. As a matter of policy, students are required to satisfy half of the teaching requirement within the first two years of their program. Students are encouraged to complete the teaching requirement early in their stay to eliminate conflicts with later dissertation work. The University Oral Examination must be completed at least a quarter before the degree is conferred.

value.advisingExpectations: Aligning with an advisor is an essential milestone in the PhD program and is required for making satisfactory degree progress and maintaining good standing. PhD students who do not align with an advisor by the end of their first year of study at Stanford are subject to dismissal from the program. PhD students may need to change advisors after initial alignment due to unexpected circumstances. Since an advisor is necessary for continued funding and good standing, please consult the Director of Student and Academic Services or Director of Graduate Studies as early as possible to ensure proper coordination and uninterrupted support. Additional guidance is available in this resource . Additional information regarding CS PhD advising is available on our CS website, CS PhD Advising Information.

value.A3i6E: Our Master of Science (MS) programs are terminal degree programs for those seeking advanced knowledge in a focused civil and environmental engineering discipline to pursue a career in industry or another professional degree. The MS degree is coursework-based. Our Master’s degrees are offered under the general regulations of the university as outlined in the Stanford Bulletin. The Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering offers Master’s degrees in five areas of specialization, described below. The Master’s program consists of core courses, technical electives, seminars, and unrestricted electives to deepen knowledge and learning. Many fundamental skills and bodies of knowledge are the foundation of all areas of specialization in a modern CEE graduate education. These cross-cutting courses are accessible to students in any program. Civil & Environmental Engineering Master's subplans: Atmosphere/Energy (A/E) Stanford University’s Atmosphere/Energy MS degree program bridges the gap between the two key Civil and Environmental Engineering disciplines. This program aims to mitigate atmospheric problems by optimizing the use of natural energy resources (wind, solar, hydro, geothermal, and marine resources); learning about the electrification of transportation, buildings, and industry; increasing the efficiency with which energy is used; and understanding the effects of energy technologies on the atmosphere. Environmental Engineering (EnvEng) The Environmental Engineering MS degree program emphasizes applying fundamental principles to analyze complex environmental problems and devise effective solutions. With this education, graduates of our program can deal effectively with new environmental issues as they emerge and meet the challenges created globally by increasing urbanization, population growth, and ecological degradation. Structural Engineering & Mechanics (SEM) Previously called Structural Engineering & Geomechanics, there are no changes to academic requirements for current students already admitted to Structural Engineering & Geomechanics. The Structural Engineering and Mechanics MS degree program offers courses in various areas related to structural analysis and design, geomechanics, engineering informatics, hazard risk and reliability, structural mechanics and materials, and structural sensing, monitoring, and data analytics for the built environment. Sustainable Design & Construction (SDC) The Sustainable Design and Construction MS degree program prepares students for careers in the built environment: designing, building, and managing sustainable buildings and infrastructure to maximize their lifecycle economic value and net contribution to environmental and social functions and services. Sustainable Engineered Systems (SES) The Sustainable Engineered Systems MS degree program, available exclusively in a hybrid online/on-campus format, is designed for students who want to gain advanced knowledge of the sustainability of civil and environmental engineering systems and data science along with a specialization in structural and material systems, sustainable construction systems, environmental engineering systems, or atmospheric and energy systems.

value.ItCSB: The purpose of the master’s program is to equip students with the knowledge and skills necessary for a successful professional career or the pursuit of doctoral studies. Students are prepared through coursework organized into three broad areas: the built environment, atmosphere and energy, and environmental engineering. Graduate students must master the analytical, quantitative, and interpretive skills necessary for successful leadership in their chosen field.
value.advisingExpectations: Faculty advisors serve as intellectual and professional mentors to graduate students. They are expected to provide knowledgeable support concerning policies for graduate studies, help prepare their students to be competitive for employment, maintain a high level of professionalism, and establish expectations concerning advisor/advisee relationships consistent with university and department standards. General university policies on advising and the conduct of research can be found on VPGE’s Advising Initiative website. Master’s students are assigned academic program advisors at the start of their program. A master’s student can request a change of advisor provided the change of advisor is made within the same program. The student is expected to inform their old and new academic advisors and the department’s student services office of such a change. Master’s students are expected to meet with their academic program advisors regularly to discuss their degree plan. MS students are encouraged to prepare a list of classes they would like to take before meeting with their advisor. Students are responsible for understanding the requirements of their degree program and working with their MS program advisor and the CEE Student Services team to ensure they are meeting degree requirements. They are empowered to request an appointment with their advisor at any time throughout the school year to discuss any problems with their studies or changes in their academic plans. If they have difficulty meeting with their advisor, they can ask the student services team or the directors of graduate studies for advice or assistance.
value.cotermTransferPolicy: In this master’s program, courses taken during or after the first quarter of the sophomore year are eligible for consideration for transfer to the graduate career; the timing of the first graduate quarter is not a factor. No courses taken before the first quarter of the sophomore year may be used to meet master’s degree requirements.
value.programGradingPolicies: Grading policies vary based on subplan. Please see the individual subplan pages for additional information. Each program has limits on the number of non-graded units. Consult with your advisor as to the maximum units acceptable in your program for courses with the grade types of S/NC or CR/NC.
value.programGPARequirement: To be able to confer any graduate degree in Civil and Environmental Engineering, students must achieve a GPA of at least 3.0 in the Stanford courses counted toward their degree.
value.programAdditionalPolicies: Students admitted to graduate study with a BS in Civil Engineering, or equivalent, from an accredited curriculum can satisfy the requirements for the MS degree in Civil and Environmental Engineering by completing a minimum of 45 units beyond the BS. All 45 units must be taken at Stanford. A minimum 3.0 grade point average (GPA) is required for candidates to be recommended for the MS degree. All CEE MS programs are course-based, and no thesis is required. The faculty of the department must approve the program of study. It should include at least 45 units of courses in engineering, mathematics, science, and related fields unless it can be shown that other work is pertinent to the student’s objectives. At least 30 units must be at the graduate level (courses numbered 200 or above) and at least 24 units must be from the School of Engineering. In addition, each of the CEE program areas has specific coursework and requirements designed to ensure the course of study has sufficient focus on appropriate CEE topics. No thesis is required for the Master’s degree. Units earned in courses below the 100-level are not accepted toward the minimum requirements for the MS degree. Non-technical courses, such as remedial English-language instruction (those checked as required on the Report on English Screening), music courses, or physical education courses, may not be included in the 45 units of required course work. Students may take any courses they wish beyond the 45 program units. Additional program area requirements are available on the department website. Candidates for the MS in Civil and Environmental Engineering who do not have a BS in Civil Engineering may, in addition to the above, be required to complete those undergraduate courses deemed essential to their graduate programs. Graduate Units and Residency Requirement Each graduate degree at Stanford has a unit-based residency requirement . The MS degree requires 45 units that must be completed at Stanford. The CEE graduate degree programs place further restrictions on the specific course work or combination of course work, research, and thesis units required for each graduate degree. All units counted towards graduate degrees in CEE must be from courses at or above the 100-level. Program Proposal for a Master’s Degree No degree can be recommended for conferral unless a Program Proposal for a Master’s Degree has been filed and represents an accurate program of study. Meet with your advisor during your first quarter of graduate study to agree upon a proposed program of coursework. All students must submit a Program Proposal for a Master’s Degree by the end of their first quarter in the program. If your actual course work changes after submitting the Program Proposal for a Master’s Degree, you must submit an updated proposal that will be reviewed for approval by your academic advisor and the department. This form must also be submitted before the end of the second week of the final quarter of your program of study to verify that no changes to the proposed coursework have been made. You should also discuss changes to your proposed plan with your advisor whenever they occur to ensure that your modified course of study still satisfies the program requirements. For coterminal students, the university requires that the graduate advisor be assigned in the student’s first graduate quarter even though the undergraduate career may still be open. The university also requires that the Master’s Degree Program Proposal be completed by the student and approved by the department by the end of the student’s first graduate quarter. Requirements for Remaining in Good Academic Standing in CEE Students enrolled for 11 or more units must pass at least 8 units per term that count toward their degree by the end of each term. Those registered for 8-10 units must pass at least 6 units per term that count toward their degree by the end of each term MS students must enroll in at least one course offered by the CEE department each quarter to remain in good academic standing. Program Duration International students must complete their CEE MS program by Spring Quarter of their second year. The CEE department does not approve I-20 extensions. International students will only be approved to be on a Leave of Absence for one quarter during their program. U.S. Citizens must complete their CEE MS degree within three years, and honors cooperative students (HCP) must complete their CEE MS degree within five years.

value.A3i6E: Welcome to Design! The DESIGN-MS bulletin outlines 2026-2027 degree requirements for students pursuing the Master of Science degree (MS) from the School of Engineering . The master's degree is only offered to active students admitted through Graduate Admissions . The degree is administered by the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford (The Stanford d.school). 100% completion of all degree requirements within this engineering program, along with meeting Graduate Academic Progress , can lead to the conferral of the Master of Science in Design (DESIGN-MS). Master of Science (MS) Design students (nicknamed Loftees) will develop a strong practice in human-centered design abilities, making, creativity, and applied project work in their chosen domain. The first year foregrounds a structured design practice that pushes to stretch intellectually and grow their skills as makers across mediums. Students will advance in focus through choosing one method and identify a domain focus. A Method will allow students to gain a depth of practice in a select set of mediums. The Domain area will allow exploring challenges in different disciplines where designers can have an impact, and where there are increasing academic and professional opportunities. The degree prepares students for further study in design, design careers in public or private sector institutions, entrepreneurial endeavors, and even careers that may not yet exist.
value.WOZxr: MS Design does not accept any external credit towards degree requirements.
value.ItCSB: The DESIGN-MS program has a foundation of four pillars: Make, Care, Adapt, and Spark [1] MAKE: The knowledge and ability to prototype and make across a wide range of mediums, existing and emerging. Students can contextualize and apply design principles across disciplinary domains. They have broad material literacy and can build and analyze in many mediums, like physical products, code, policy, and emerging technologies. Learning goals: Experiment rapidly at low resolution using a wide range of physical and digital mediums Recognize emerging technologies that may impact design work Build professional fluency in a subset of design methodologies Investigate needs and opportunities in multi-stakeholder systems Apply foundational design abilities and processes to challenges in other disciplines [2] CARE: The care and responsibility to be leading stewards of the planet, all people, and the data we generate. Students know how to work slowly and fast, with appreciation and respect for varying time scales of change. They learn from and with other humans and the environment. They realize the importance of equity, ethics, and implications. They prioritize people and the planet over profit. Learning goals: Scope a design project that meets a societal or planetary need in relation to the context, constraints, time scale, and opportunities of the problem space Use equitable and inclusive research approaches focused on learning from/with others Predict implications, and impact, of work on complete systems and alternative approaches Consider ethical questions and implications to design work on multiple time horizons Integrate historical, environmental, cultural, and contextual awareness into design work [3] ADAPT: The flexibility of adaptive learners. Students can synthesize and integrate ideas and experiences from across the different aspects of their Stanford education and beyond. They can articulate their capacity and needs as learners when tackling open-ended problems. As emerging leaders, they can establish the conditions for others’ creativity to emerge. Learning goals: Navigate ambiguous projects and processes with appropriate methods Develop a reflective practice on past learning and work to consolidate skills and knowledge Integrate learning from a wide range of life experiences to develop habits and mindsets that foster life-long learning and essential preparation for tackling emergent design opportunities Overcome emotional or intellectual disorientation or discomfort in individual and team contexts when faced with the unknown [4] SPARK: The quirky creativity that produces new world ideas. Students see trends, spot new opportunities, and have the courage to try something untested boldly. They relish disciplinary intersections, embrace ambiguity, and can collaborate and communicate with diverse people. They can set visions and paths for them. Learning goals: Synthesize information from disparate sources, quantitative and qualitative Create design experiments that utilize engineering and scientific principles to evaluate the efficacy and impact of new-to-the-world ideas Move fluidly between abstract ideas and concrete details on design projects Collaborate and communicate as a member of a multidisciplinary design team Communicate deliberately with a range of audiences in a variety of storytelling media
value.advisingExpectations: You will be assigned one Faculty Advisor upon entering the program. This person will serve as your primary advisor for check-ins, questions, course planning and inquiries. value.programAdditionalPolicies: Degree Requirements: You must follow degree requirements from a year that overlaps your matriculation. You may not double-count classes across any degree category. All units must be in courses at or above the 100 level (units earned in courses below the 100 level may not count towards the minimum unit requirement for the master’s degree). Methods : You should choose your Method by the end of your first quarter. Domains : You should identify your Domain, and all classes for it, by the end of your first year. Curricular Practical Training (CPT) : Design abides by Curricular Practical Training guidance from Bechtel International Center. You are permitted 2 uses of CPT in MS Design . You must enroll in DESIGN 391A if utilizing CPT. Petitions and Deviations : You must discuss any petition inquiry with a Faculty Advisor first before filling out the Design: Petition Form . You should submit petition requests at least one quarter ahead of time. You may not have retroactive, or same-quarter requests, considered so plan ahead. You should allow at least three weeks for petitions to be reviewed. You should plan with allowed classes so as to not be unprepared by a petition denial. You may not have petitions considered in the quarter you intend to confer. Independent Study : You must enroll in DESIGN 391 if utilizing Graduate Independent Study and Research. Any intention for Independent Study to go towards degree requirements is considered rare and needs petition approval first.

Graduate study in electrical engineering requires that students be adequately prepared in circuits, digital systems, fields, lab work, mathematics, and physics. Students should typically be able to complete the master’s degree in five quarters; note that most courses are not offered during the Summer. In planning a course of study, it is the student’s responsibility, in consultation with an advisor, to determine whether the prerequisites for advanced courses have been met. Prerequisite courses ordinarily taken by undergraduates may be included as part of the graduate program of study. However, if the number of these is large, the proposed program may contain more than the minimum 45 units, and the time required to meet the degree requirements may be increased. The master’s degree program provides advanced preparation for professional practice or junior college-level teaching. Faculty are assigned as program advisors to guide course selection and exploration of academic opportunities and professional pathways. The program proposal must be submitted to the Degree Progress Officer before the end of the first quarter of graduate study (second quarter for Honors Cooperative Program students); a final revised version is due at the beginning of the last quarter of study, before degree conferral. value.A3i6E: The Electrical Engineering PhD degree is designed to prepare students for careers in research and teaching at the university level. The PhD in Electrical Engineering is a specialized degree built on a broad science, mathematics, and engineering skills base. The course program must reflect competency in Electrical Engineering and specialized study in other areas relevant to the student’s research focus. Students should discuss their course selection with their dissertation advisor. The University’s basic requirements for the PhD degree are outlined here. Department requirements are stated below. Students in the PhD program must complete the following requirements: (1) a qualifying examination given by the faculty of the Department of Electrical Engineering; (2) an approved program of study in Electrical Engineering and allied subjects; (3) an approved topic of research and a written dissertation, based on research, which must be a significant contribution to knowledge; (4) and an oral examination that is a defense of dissertation research and is taken near the completion of the doctoral program. See the Electrical Engineering Department website for complete requirements and additional information, Financial Assistance The Department awards a limited number of fellowships, teaching and course assistantships, and research assistantships to incoming graduate students. Applying for financial assistance is part of the admission application.

value.advisingExpectations: See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. The Department of Electrical Engineering is committed to providing academic advising in support of doctoral student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by both advisor and advisee. Students are expected to meet with their PhD dissertation advisor at least once per year. Students who do not have a dissertation advisor are encouraged to check in with their program advisor. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both advisor and advisee are expected to maintain professionalism, respect, and integrity. They should also be responsive to one another promptly. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The Department’s Graduate Handbook provides information and suggested timelines for different stages of the doctoral program. For more information, see the department’s Graduate Degree Progress website. PhD students are initially assigned a program advisor based on the interests expressed in their application. This faculty member provides initial guidance in course selection, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and identifying doctoral research opportunities. The department does not require formal lab rotations, but students are encouraged to consider exploring research activities in two or three labs during their first academic year. Students identify their doctoral research/thesis advisor, pass the qualifying exam, and advance to candidacy before the end of the second year of study. The research supervisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most students find an advisor from among the primary faculty members of the department. The research advisor may alternatively be a faculty member from another Stanford department familiar with supervising doctoral students and can provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program. When the research advisor is from outside the department, the student still maintains the previous program advisor from the primary faculty to guide departmental requirements and opportunities. The EE Associate Chair of Graduate Education is available during the academic year by email and during office hours. The department’s student services office is also an essential part of the doctoral advising team: they inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and they maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. Students are encouraged to talk with their doctoral program advisor, the Graduate Student Teaching Advisor, and the Degree Progress Officer from the student services office as they consider advisor selection or for guidance in working with their advisor(s). The department’s doctoral students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. See the Electrical Engineering Department Graduate Handbook (pdf) for more information. ALIGNING AND CHANGING DISSERTATION ADVISORS Aligning with an advisor is an essential milestone in the PhD program and is required for making satisfactory degree progress and maintaining good standing. Students are able to rotate during autumn, winter, and spring quarters of their first year. Research rotations are meant to allow students to engage in research within labs, explore research areas, and meet other potential advisors. The EE Department manages an optional rotation program in the autumn quarter for incoming EE PhD students. For winter and spring quarters, students must schedule their own rotations. EE PhD students are expected to align with an advisor at the end of their first year. Upon aligning with an advisor, students transition from department fellowship to advisor-provided funding. Therefore, students must select an advisor who can financially support them. PhD students who do not align with an advisor by the spring quarter of their second year of study at Stanford are subject to dismissal from the program. A student who does not align with an advisor by the stated deadline is considered to be “on academic notice” as a warning of unsatisfactory degree progress. The student's progress and efforts will be closely monitored to ensure that they align with an advisor on a reasonable timeline during the quarter of notice. If a student requires an additional quarter, a faculty committee will meet to review the case and decide on possible outcomes. If a student has not aligned with an advisor by the spring quarter of their second year, a possible consequence includes the termination of a student’s study toward a PhD in Electrical Engineering; however, the student may continue to work toward an MS degree. Departmental PhD financial support does not continue. PhD students may need to change advisors after initial alignment due to various circumstances. Since an advisor is necessary for continued funding and good standing, please consult the Electrical Engineering Student Services team as early as possible to ensure proper coordination and uninterrupted support. Additional guidance for students considering an advisor change is available in this resource . If a student needs to change advisors, the Department requires the student to actively seek and find a new advisor within one quarter, to satisfy minimum progress requirements of the Department and the University and to continue enrolling. If the student is unable to secure a new advisor by the end of the quarter, the Department will initiate procedures for dismissal per the “ Guidelines for Dismissal of Graduate Students for Academic or Professional Reasons ” in the Stanford Bulletin.

value.A3i6E: The Department of Materials Science and Engineering is concerned with designing, making, and characterizing new materials that will have societal impact. Materials science and engineering is an interdisciplinary field involving the relationships between structure and properties of materials and how to take advantage of them in applications. Our students and faculty do research down to the infinitesimally small to achieve breakthroughs of global significance, working at the atomic and molecular levels to engineer matter that will enable the materials, devices, and systems essential for cutting-edge solar energy production, energy storage, information technology, medicine, and more. The Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) program is designed to give students a broad and deep understanding of materials science and engineering so that they will have long and fruitful careers as researchers or teachers at the university level. Students who graduate from our program will be among the world’s leading experts in the areas of their dissertation research. They also will have the intellectual tools to move into new research areas as the field grows and develops. The University’s basic requirements for the PhD degree are outlined in the Graduate Degrees section of the Bulletin. Department requirements are stated below. See the Materials Science and Engineering Department website for more information.

value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Mechanical Engineering (ME) is committed to academic advising to support graduate students’ scholarly and professional development. This advising relationship is most effective when it entails collaborative and sustained engagement between the advisor and the advisee. The advisor/advisee relationship and expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed as a best practice to ensure mutual understanding. All advisors and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Faculty advisors guide graduate students in critical areas of their academic careers. An academic advisor helps guide student selection of courses and provides help in navigating policies and degree requirements. In the case of faculty advising teaching assistants, the relationship should include assistance with teaching pedagogy and practice development. If the advisor also serves as the primary research advisor, then the advising is much more extensive and includes research training, design, execution, and career planning (see also PhD section below). In all cases, graduate students should be active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program (including reading the ME Department’s Graduate Student Handbook). Graduate students conducting research should also strive to understand the method and goals of the research and the project’s contribution to the pertinent field. The faculty Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) meets with all master’s and doctoral students at the start of their first year and is available year-round via email and by appointment. The department’s Student Services Office is also an essential part of the advising team; they inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities and maintain the official records of advising assignments. Students are encouraged to talk with the staff of the Student Services Office, including the DGS, as they consider advisor selection or for advice in working with their advisor(s). Another excellent resource for students is the ME Graduate Student Committee. This student-run group organizes social, academic, and community events for the graduate student population in the ME Department. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. PhD and Engineer Degrees The ME Department provides academic advising in support of doctoral student scholarly and professional development. A successful advisor/advisee relationship is significant for students seeking a PhD in the department. The material in this section also applies to students pursuing the Engineer degree. In addition to the goals listed above for all advisor/advisee relationships, the PhD advisor provides advice and guidance on developing research skills, choosing classes that help with the student’s research, identifying and planning research projects, dissemination/publishing the research, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The PhD advisor serves as the PhD student’s intellectual and professional mentor. Sometimes, a PhD student may be advised by two or more advisors. In these cases, each individual’s roles and goals should be made very clear to all involved. For example, the co-advisors in such arrangements should strive to coordinate and provide non-conflicting advice to the student. The advisee should work to improve and facilitate communication with the two advisors and provide feedback to and from their advisors. In the ME department, PhD students can be admitted to be advised by a specified faculty member or accepted with a fellowship associated with the research rotation program. For the latter, the department initially assigns the student a program advisor. This faculty member provides initial guidance in course selection, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and identifying doctoral research opportunities. Students are required to perform rotations until a PhD research advisor is identified, and they are strongly encouraged to explore research activities with two or three different faculty members during their first academic year. All PhD students seeking a PhD research advisor are encouraged to actively seek out, meet with, and discuss possibilities for PhD advisors. Ideally, these discussions should include possible research projects and the potential for and sources of sustained research funding. PhD students must identify their doctoral research/thesis advisor (and vice versa) before the first year of study ends. Ideally, this should happen within the first nine to ten months. The research supervisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and the aforementioned research-related advice and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most ME PhD students find an advisor from the department’s primary faculty members. However, the research advisor may be a qualified faculty member from another Stanford department who can provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program . When the research advisor is from outside the department, the student must also identify a program advisor, called a co-advisor, from the primary ME faculty to guide departmental requirements and opportunities. The co-advisor is also a member of the student’s dissertation reading committee. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

value.A3i6E: The MS degree program represents substantial progress in the major field beyond the bachelor’s degree. Students must complete at least 45 units at Stanford in courses numbered 100 and above. See Graduate Degrees for university requirements for the master’s degree. Coterminal master’s degree candidates are expected to complete all master’s degree requirements as described in this Bulletin. MS&E master’s students complete breadth as well as depth in MS&E; depth possibilities include: Data, AI, and Decisions: Courses in Data, AI, and Decisions prepare students in the fundamentals of data and decision sciences, machine learning, and artificial intelligence that are transforming operational and strategic decision making in information technology, finance, healthcare, services, manufacturing, and government. The program combines rigorous technical foundations with emerging modern applications. Financial Analytics: Courses in Financial Analytics prepare students for careers requiring analytical rigor and the ability to innovate around market challenges. Example career paths include financial services, risk management, investment management, financial technology and data processing, financial regulation and policy, exchanges and clearing houses, and auditing and compliance. Courses combine the in-depth study of quantitative techniques with practical, hands-on business problem-solving. Students learn to use mathematical models and quantitative tools to solve complex problems in finance practice, exploiting the intellectual ties between finance, operations research, computer science, and engineering. It offers a high level of flexibility and a range of elective courses that allow students to tailor the program to their specific career goals. Required courses immerse students in quantitative methods and deepen their understanding of finance fundamentals. Projects courses feature practical, data-driven team projects and case studies, fostering group learning and peer interaction. Technology and Engineering Management: Courses in Technology and Engineering Management prepare students for careers including product and project management, management consulting, and entrepreneurship. They acquire skills to manage technical organizations, foster innovation, and deal with rapidly evolving technologies and dynamic markets. Specialized coursework is flexible, allowing students to explore and gain depth and understanding of technical organizations to develop a culture of successful innovation and entrepreneurship, along with decision-making methods under uncertainty, financial analysis, and strategic planning. Technology Policy: Courses in Technology Policy focus on the design and analysis of public policies and corporate strategies, especially those with technology-based issues. It features a grounding in microeconomics and modeling approaches. Courses with a policy focus include such topics such as national security, energy and environment, and health care. Students may also self-design a depth area; possibilities for a self-designed depth area include: Computational Social Science: Courses in Computational Social Science teach students how to apply rigorous statistical and computational methods to address problems in economics, sociology, political science, and beyond. Students are prepared for diverse career paths in data science, information technology, and policy analysis. Coursework covers fundamental statistical concepts, large-scale computation, and network analysis. Students can explore topics such as experimental design, algorithmic economics, and machine learning through electives. Decision Analysis and Risk Analysis: Courses in Decision and Risk Analysis prepare students for careers including management consulting, policy analysis, and risk management, applying engineering systems analysis to tackle complex economic and technical management problems in the private and public sectors. They acquire the skills to identify and develop opportunities in uncertain situations while recognizing and hedging the downside risks. Specialized coursework includes the mathematical foundations for modeling in dynamic, uncertain environments to value and manage uncertain opportunities and risks, applications to public policy, and a chance to work on a client project under faculty guidance. Recommended courses include MS&E 250A, 250B, 252, and 355. Energy and Environment: Courses in Energy and Environment are designed for students interested in energy and environmental issues from the perspectives of public policy, non-governmental organizations, or corporations. Recommended courses include MS&E 241, 243, and 394, CEE 207A, 273S, and ENERGY 201A, 201B, 201C, 223, 240, 241, 281 and 291. Health Systems Modeling: Courses in Health Systems Modeling are designed for students interested in health care operations and policy. Courses emphasize applying mathematical and economic analysis to problems in public health policy and the design and operation of health care services. Recommended courses include MS&E 263, 292, and 463, and HRP 263 and 392.

value.ItCSB: The master’s in Management Science and Engineering prepares engineers for a lifelong career addressing private and public organizations’ technical and managerial needs. The program emphasizes developing analytic abilities, making better decisions, and developing and executing strategies while also leading people who innovate. MS&E students know math, engineering, as well as behavioral science. They can conduct experiments to design better systems, organizations, and work processes. They understand how to analyze data to solve real-world problems. They can develop mathematical and computational models to inform action. They know how to surface and examine unarticulated assumptions and root causes. These students can communicate effectively in the team environments found in so many contemporary organizations.

facts.value: Individually Designed MA in Education is intended for current Stanford doctoral students in a PhD outside GSE. Admission follows GSE consultation and an individualized plan; complete 45 units including at least 27 GSE units within three years, then file Graduate Authorization Petition.
conditions: Not an external entry route.

facts.value: GSE takes a limited number of Stanford undergraduates into MA/MS coterm study after at least 120 units toward graduation; undergraduate department approval and GSE admission both required.

GSE MA specializations include Curriculum and Teacher Education, Global and Comparative Education, International Education Policy Analysis, Policy, Organization and Leadership Studies, plus joint MA/MBA, MA/JD and MA/MPP. MS offerings include Education Data Science and Learning, Design, and Technology. STEP is a 12-month MA with preliminary California credential; GSE also lists Teaching of Physics MA.
conditions: Bulletin award rows group specializations; current admissions route must be checked per track.

facts.value: For 2027-28 entry, GSE PhD deadline is November 16, 2026; MA/MS deadline is January 7, 2027. Knight-Hennessy applicants to GSE must separately meet the November 16, 2026 KHS program deadline.

GRE is not required for 2027-28; applicants may submit optional scores without penalty. Applicants not meeting the central English exemption must meet GSE minimum TOEFL iBT 100 before Jan 21 2026 or 5 after that date, or IELTS Academic 7.5.

Core GSE application asks for 1-2 page single-spaced 12-point statement of purpose, resume/CV, three recommendations, and transcripts from every college/university attended at least one full-time academic year. Upload PDFs/scanned records; current in-progress transcript accepted before degree conferral. Foreign-language transcripts need complete literal translation; admitted students later send official records.
conditions: The general Education MA option represents shared ordinary GSE MA guidance only. STEP, individually designed MA, closed CTE intake and joint GSB/Law/POLS-forwarded routes use their own application instructions. Selecting a named variant must not inherit this checklist by parent degree alone.

facts.value: Doctoral program committees may interview. Writing sample is not required for CTE, DAPS, LSTD, or Economics of Education; required 10+ page research-oriented samples for Anthropology of Education, Educational Linguistics, History of Education, Global and Comparative Education, Philosophy of Education; required research samples for EDS, Higher Education, Sociology of Education and RILE. LSTD and RILE applicants under SHIPS must apply to that area and another SHIPS subplan. RILE sample topic must relate to race, inequality and/or language; 1,000-5,000 words preferred. The History/Social Science Education PhD area will not admit for 2027-28.
conditions: Some area committees may interview; others state no interview.

facts.value: DAPS, Economics of Education, Education Data Science, Educational Policy, Higher Education, and Sociology of Education specify supplemental essays/skills questions; respond to each area-specific prompt on the GSE page.

For 2027-28: CTE MA will not admit. EDS MS has no writing sample or interview but requires supplemental essays/skills matrix and basic programming experience/coursework; LDT MS has no writing sample/interview and uses a program-specific statement and short answers. GCE/IEPA MA requires an English research writing sample of at least 10 pages and track-specific statement. POLS MA requires a writing sample up to 10 pages and supplemental essays.
conditions: CTE closure applies to the stated 2027-28 cycle only.

facts.value: STEP applicants choose Elementary or one of five Secondary subject areas (English, history/social science, math, science, world languages). The 12-month full-time program leads to MA plus preliminary California teaching credential. STEP requires a 750-1,250 word essay (max 3 pages), resume, three recommendations, and transcripts for each institution attended at least one year. Current page contains inconsistent 2026-27/2027 cohort term references; follow current application and the 2027-28 MA deadline.
conditions: The historical cycle/start-term mismatch needs live application confirmation.

facts.value: MFA applicants submit an online SlideRoom portfolio by deadline; $10 SlideRoom fee. Include typed work list with date, medium, size, title and viewing instructions. Still-image total max 20; time-based selection max 10 minutes (preferred excerpt 5 minutes). SOP no more than two pages; first sentence must name program and area. Three references, postsecondary transcripts for each full-time institution attended at least one academic year. GRE not required; department states TOEFL for applicants whose first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted, while current central exemptions apply.
conditions: Art & Art History page says TOEFL is required when the applicant’s first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted; central Graduate Admissions lists TOEFL or IELTS and exemptions. Confirm which stricter rule the Art Practice application currently enforces.

facts.value: Autumn-only entry, December 1 at 9 p.m. Pacific deadline; all materials including tests/recommendations/portfolio must arrive by deadline. Department normally provides support package through fellowship plus teaching assistantships, including tuition support, salary and small materials grants; two-year full-time program, typically admits up to five yearly.
conditions: Finalists must travel to Stanford for late-February faculty/student interview. Funding wording is typical/normal rather than guaranteed individual award.

facts.value: Submit one 5-8 page analytical essay on a documentary film/topic as PDF; submit SlideRoom portfolio with film/video work where applicant had creative control if possible. Total sample runtime max 15 minutes, with synopsis, clip runtime and applicant role; minimal production experience may be represented by strongest work in another visual medium. No production-assistant-only work. SlideRoom fee is $6. SOP max two pages; three recommendations and transcripts for institutions attended full-time for at least one year.

Autumn 2027-28 application materials due December 1 at 9 p.m. Pacific; no midyear entry. Two consecutive years in residence. First year fellowship includes stipend and tuition; second-year TA eligibility includes salary and tuition allowance. Production funds also offered.
conditions: Second-year TA support is eligibility, not guaranteed award.

facts.value: Music PhD/DMA applicants must hold a bachelor’s degree; PhD/DMA applicants are expected to have preparation equivalent to a Music bachelor’s. Terminal MA Music, Science, and Technology targets applicants with undergraduate engineering, science, music, arts, or a degree including engineering mathematics. Application requires SOP, three recommendations, unofficial transcripts for each school attended at least one year; MA/PhD also require scholarly writing sample. DMA composition adds complete composition list and links to representative scores and 3-6 audio/video recordings.

GRE is optional for all Music graduate programs. Application for September entry opens late September/early October; completed application due the second Tuesday in December. TOEFL is required for international applicants whose primary language is not English unless they meet waiver requirements. Department does not provide its own fee waiver.
conditions: Program-specific 2027 cycle deadline is in the central directory; department page describes second-Tuesday rule.

facts.value: Doctoral-level Music applicants are expected to have preparation equivalent to a bachelor’s in Music; department suggests comparing prior study to Stanford Music bachelor’s requirements to identify missing theory/history preparation. After admission, incoming doctoral students take dictation and theory diagnostics; musicologists/composers take piano proficiency; ethnomusicologists take piano/other instrument proficiency or non-Western musical traditions test; musicologists take Western-art-music history/repertoire test. Deficiencies may delay TA assignment until remedied.

The terminal History MA is for students who do not intend to continue into Stanford History’s PhD; admitted terminal MA students may not apply to enter the department PhD while working on the MA. Autumn-only entry. Apply through central graduate application with statement of purpose, three recommendations, scanned transcripts for every college attended at least one year, and a 10-25 page history writing sample. GRE general is not required; confirm English testing against central 2027-28 rules. 2027-28 application deadline is December 1, 2026.

facts.value: History admits a limited number of Stanford undergraduates to the coterm MA. Applicants specify a field and faculty advisor and need 3.75 GPA in History courses (or equivalent preparation if not a History major). Requirements include coterm application, statement, Stanford transcript, 10-25 page history sample, three recommendations (at least two from History faculty; one from current advisor and one from prospective MA advisor), preliminary program proposal and course-transfer information. Spring-quarter entry only; 2026-27 deadline December 1, 2026. Courses cannot double-count toward both degrees.
conditions: Coterm admissions are an internal undergraduate route and must not be treated as external terminal admission.

facts.value: History guarantees five years of continuous 12-month funding for doctoral students who remain actively enrolled and in good academic standing. Package combines fellowship and assistantship support and provides tuition, stipend/salary, summer stipend and health insurance. Students may separately apply for relocation, conference-travel and research grants.
conditions: Five-year guarantee has active-enrollment and good-standing conditions.

facts.value: EALC applicants need at least three years of training in the language of intended specialization; a prior EALC undergraduate major is not required. Applicants must seek graduate study in a scholarly field (e.g., literature/culture, linguistics, archaeology or Trans-Asian studies), not merely language acquisition.

EALC MA requires a research/writing sample of approximately 15 pages and three recommendations; applicants upload transcripts and the department may contact finalists for Zoom interviews. Students normally complete 45 units and enroll in at least 8 units each quarter. EALC provides limited tuition fellowships to admitted MA students and encourages outside funding.
conditions: Three recommendations, writing sample and transcript requirements apply to the EALC MA route.

facts.value: EALC offers five years of 12-month PhD funding through fellowship, research-assistantship and teaching-assistantship support; students are encouraged to seek outside fellowships.

Comparative Literature PhD: scholarly literary-critical/analytic sample about 5,000 words in English; creative writing is not a substitute. French and Italian graduate programs: two 20-page samples, one in English and one in French or Italian. German Studies: approximately 5,000 words of scholarly analysis in German or English. Iberian and Latin American Cultures: two 20-page samples, one English and one Spanish. Slavic Languages and Literatures: about 20 pages in English analyzing Slavic texts; a short Russian or other relevant-language sample is optional.

Slavic PhD students are required to learn/read Russian, one quarter of Old Church Slavonic, and at least two other languages relevant to research (often French, German or another Slavic language, with alternatives depending on research interests).

Classics PhD application asks for an academic paper in the field, 15-25 pages, and a CV listing language qualifications; ancient-language preparation should be demonstrated by works read in the original and modern-language proficiency may be described by level and years studied. The department says a strong Classics or related-field background is expected.
conditions: Department page’s English-test wording should be reconciled with current university exemption and accepted-test policy.

facts.value: English PhD deadline is December 1, 2026. Submit a critical/scholarly writing sample 12-25 pages (excluding references), preferably in intended area and clear of grading comments. Statement should ideally be 500-600 words and may not exceed 1,000 words.

The 2026-27 Bulletin has a Classics MA degree row, while the Classics Graduate Admissions page states that its MA has been discontinued. The current external directory does not list a Classics MA entry.
conditions: The official current admissions page says discontinued.

facts.value: The application originates with GSB MBA Admissions. Applicants select interest in the joint program in the MBA application and complete an additional essay. Current MBA1 students may apply during their first quarter using the internal joint application. The program is two years full-time.

Apply through the GSE POLS MA application, indicate MA/MPP consideration and complete the joint-degree prompt. If admitted to POLS, GSE forwards the application to Public Policy; POLS admission is required, but MPP admission is separate. Econ 1 and Math 20 are required before matriculation, though not necessarily at application.
conditions: Both programs try to issue concurrent decisions, but timing may differ; final decisions precede April 15.

facts.value: Applicants may apply through the Law School and indicate joint MA/JD interest, or apply after Law School admission before the earlier of the end of JD year two or the GSE deadline for the intended MA start. Both schools must approve the joint course of study.

The History of Art MA is only available to Art & Art History PhD students as progress toward the PhD. The department does not admit students who want only the MA. The PhD field may include Film & Media Studies; doctoral students also complete collateral studies in another graduate department or interdisciplinary program.

Submit three recommendation letters; scanned transcripts for each postsecondary institution attended full-time for at least one academic year; and an SOP of no more than 1,000 words, single spaced, 12-point Times New Roman, 1-inch margins, naming the PhD program and field in its first sentence. One writing sample of at most 20 pages including illustrations and bibliography; full master’s theses are not accepted. GRE is not required. Finalists may be interviewed by faculty via Skype. Autumn-only admission; department page gives December 1, 9 p.m. Pacific deadline and decisions around March 15.
conditions: Department page says TOEFL required when first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted; reconcile with central university policy and exemption criteria.
exceptions: Department deadline page says 9 p.m. Pacific while central Graduate Admissions permits submission by 11:59 p.m. Pacific; verify the stricter department cutoff in live application.

facts.value: Art History PhD normally has a five-year support package from departmental fellowships, teaching and research assistantships; additional support includes summer language study, summer research, and individual research/travel funds. Students select a particular art-history field (including Film & Media Studies), complete collateral graduate study; progress review occurs at end of year two, dissertation topic/proposal by end of year three, and dissertation must be completed within five years after candidacy.
conditions: Support is described as normal rather than a guaranteed award; candidacy completion starts a separate five-year dissertation clock.

facts.value: For 2027-28 GSE coterm entry, Stanford undergraduates need at least 120 units toward graduation, apply to one coterm program per term, and submit the coterm application, preliminary program proposal, statement of purpose, resume, undergraduate transcript and two recommendations. GRE is not required. Deadline January 7, 2027; decisions in early March; accepted applicants respond by April 15, 2027 before completion of their undergraduate degree. The CTE MA accepts no applications for this cycle.

GSE masters programs are largely self-funded. The 2026-27 published cost-of-attendance page gives program-specific budgets for GCE/IEPA, LDT, POLS and EDS; EDS year-two 2027-28 figures are estimates. No one school-wide price applies to STEP or the joint degrees. All domestic and international applicants are automatically considered for Deans Fellowships; the award is included with the admission offer if granted and is final. Zaentz fellowship consideration for EDS, GCE/IEPA, LDT and POLS requires separate early-childhood responses in the online application.

GSE offers all admitted Education PhD students a five-year package of tuition aid, fellowship stipend and assistantship salary covering the standard cost of attendance for the student alone. Assistantship work is part of the package; this is not a funding promise for GSE masters or joint-degree applicants.

Education Data Science MS is a two-year full-time residential program with at least 51 units. It combines coursework in education and data science with an internship and mentored original research projects; its duration and cost cannot be inferred from the one-year MA/MS tracks.

Global and Comparative Education and International Education Policy Analysis are two tracks of a 48-unit MA. Both complete an MA research paper through the EDUC 206 series; GCE and IEPA have distinct track requirements. The program includes summer enrollment.

Learning Design and Technology MS requires at least 45 units, including at least 30 GSE units, over the academic year and summer. It includes internship workshops in at least two quarters, a learning portfolio and a masters design project.

Policy, Organization and Leadership Studies MA requires at least 45 units, including at least 27 GSE units, across Autumn through Spring. Its 2026-27 field placement involves about 150 hours and a project deliverable.

STEP Secondary admits by the intended credential subject: English, history/social science, mathematics, science or world languages. Candidates complete at least 45 units over four quarters, student teaching alongside coursework, an Education MA and a preliminary California single-subject teaching credential.

The Division of Literatures, Cultures, and Languages states all admitted PhD students receive five years of 12-month funding through tuition/fellowship and research or teaching assistantships; its programs do not provide financial support to masters students. Division departments do not grant their own application fee waivers; applicants may review central university waiver routes. The division page currently labels its admission cycle ambiguously, so no deadline is inferred here.

English PhD admits receive five years of 12-month support through fellowship and assistantships, with non-guaranteed sixth-year consideration. PhD candidates demonstrate reading knowledge of one foreign language; the department prefers evidence before admission. Teaching includes a first-year pedagogy seminar and typically three teaching assignments.

Modern Thought and Literature PhD requests a purpose statement no longer than 1,500 words explaining interdisciplinary preparation and a scholarly critical/analytic writing sample of at most 7,000 words; creative writing is not a substitute. No particular undergraduate major is required. Admitted students receive a five-year plan covering tuition and stipend/salary, including five summers.

The Modern Thought and Literature coterm MA is for current Stanford undergraduates well prepared in literature and at least one foreign language, including students from other majors. Its application asks for a roughly 20-page analytical writing sample and is due January 13, 2027.

Religious Studies PhD applicants specify a field, provide an SOP of at most five double-spaced pages, three confidential recommendations, transcripts and a 15-25 page double-spaced English academic writing sample on religion preceded by a short rationale. GRE is optional. Faculty consider prior religious-studies and research-language preparation and fit with faculty resources. Decisions normally arrive late February; offers may be accepted through April 15.

Religious Studies PhD students are eligible for up to five years of funding, including tuition, student Cardinal Care insurance, stipend or teaching assistantships, plus up to five funded summers. The department does not fund coterminal or masters students.

East Asian Studies MA 2027-28 application closes December 3, 2026. External applicants select Humanities/Social Sciences method and China/Japan/Korea region; submit transcripts, three recommendations, purpose statement (recommended at most 1,000 words), and first 15 double-spaced pages of an English academic nonfiction writing sample. GRE is not considered. CEAS offers limited fellowships, contingent on availability; check yes for financial aid in the application. Coterm applicants have different recommendation requirements and are considered for CEAS fellowships only under stated enrollment rules.

Russian, East European and Eurasian Studies MA application deadline is January 12, 2027. External terminal and current Stanford undergraduate coterm applications use separate online routes. External applicants submit transcripts, an at-most-two-page purpose statement, three relevant faculty references (one preferably language instructor), a writing sample of no more than 20 English pages and a list of relevant coursework with grades. Three years of relevant language study is strong preparation, but candidates with less are considered; this is not a hard minimum.

Latin American Studies MA requires Spanish at B1 CEFR/intermediate-high ACTFL or equivalent third-year university study and experience studying, working or living in Latin America/Iberia. External applicants provide a short purpose statement, 150-250 word proposed-research abstract, English academic writing sample and Spanish-fluency statement where their degree was not at a Spanish-language institution. Current Stanford undergraduates may use the coterm route after 120 units. Department fellowships and assistantships are competitive/available rather than guaranteed; applicants indicate aid interest in the online application.

Theater and Performance Studies accepts external PhD applications only, not a terminal MA. It asks for a purpose statement (at most two double-spaced pages), artistic statement (at most three), production-experience summary/CV, one or two scholarly papers totaling no more than 25 pages, transcripts and three recommendations. GRE is not required; a masters is not required. Applicants may be interviewed; decisions are communicated in March. The current official Graduate Admissions directory corroborates the November 24, 2026 deadline in the page header; the body still contains a stale November 25, 2025 date.

Theater and Performance Studies PhD describes a five-year fellowship package with tuition, health insurance, travel award and living stipend. First years emphasize full-time study; later years include teaching and dissertation writing.

Music DMA and PhD doctoral students receive five years of 12-month funding; individual Cardinal Care premiums are covered for three academic quarters in each of the five years. Later assistantships depend on department needs. The Music, Science, and Technology terminal MA does not typically receive department or center funding, although an eligible student may occasionally receive fellowship or teaching support; no award is assured. The department offers no departmental application fee waiver.

Classics PhD offers a six-year funding package conditional on satisfactory progress. Through year five the package provides stipend, tuition and health insurance for four academic quarters per year; it includes five funded summers. Applicants do not file a separate departmental funding application.

The MLA is a part-time, on-campus evening program normally lasting four or five years, with at least 50 units and an interdisciplinary thesis. Most students take one course per quarter. MLA students are not eligible for Stanford graduate housing.

The currently available MLA tuition page quotes $12,708 annual tuition for 2025-26, billed in three installments, with separate document and student-activity fees. This is historical for a 2027 applicant, not a current-cycle quote. Admission is need-blind; the MLA tuition-assistance program seeks to help students with demonstrated need after admission. Part-time MLA students generally lack traditional student-loan eligibility.

For 2027 entry, GSE plans PhD decisions in mid-February and masters/coterm decisions in early March. Responses are due April 15, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific. STEP begins June 21, 2027; other GSE PhD and masters programs begin September 20, 2027. These dates are GSE routes, not joint MBA/JD decisions.

STEP candidates need a bachelors degree before program start. California subject-matter competence may be shown through CSET, qualifying coursework, aligned degree, or approved preparation program; at least half the subject domains are due by program start and all CSET subtests by August. A foreign bachelors degree requires approved equivalency evaluation for California basic-skills credential purposes. The STEP page mixes old cohort dates; verify calendar-specific test deadlines for 2027.

STEP offers need/merit tuition fellowships of $5,000-$35,000 and a small number of full-tuition Stanford Teaching Fellows awards. Qualified future teachers may receive a forgivable loan up to $40,000 tied to teaching at an eligible U.S. school, with half forgiven after two years and the balance after four. Applicants seeking these fellowships complete the STEP supplemental funding section and FAFSA; no award is automatic.

Biology and Biophysics are two of 14 Stanford Biosciences PhD Home Programs spanning Humanities and Sciences and Medicine. They use the shared Biosciences application for Autumn 2027-28, due December 1, 2026 at 11:59:59 p.m. PST. GRE General is not considered for either; Biology does not consider a GRE Subject test, while Biophysics treats Mathematics or Physics Subject scores as optional. The applicant selects a Home Program; these two H&S awards should not be reclassified as School of Medicine awards.

Linguistics accepts only currently enrolled Stanford undergraduates to its coterm MA, not external MA applicants. For Spring 2026-27 entry, application deadline is January 12, 2027. Submit Stanford transcript, purpose statement explaining the MA and possible research paper, adviser-approved program proposal, named Linguistics faculty adviser, and three references including one Linguistics faculty member.
