published_requirement_narratives.heading: Requirements Overview
published_requirement_narratives.text: To receive the MS degree, students are expected to demonstrate knowledge of issues in health policy and the quantitative skills necessary for research in this area. List of MS Requirements: Submission of Course Plan (also known as Master's Program Proposal), approved by the primary advisor and program director, by the end of the autumn quarter of the first year Submission of Thesis Proposal , approved by the primary advisor and program director, by the end of the spring quarter of the first year Submission of Collaborative Master's Plan , after consultation with and approval of primary advisor, by November of the second year Successful completion of all course requirements , with 45 units of health-policy-related coursework (minimum) Successful completion of Master's Thesis , with approval of the student’s thesis committee Note: If a required course is not offered during a student’s time in the program, alternate plans for replacement courses can be made with the student’s advisor(s) and program director(s).

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Required Courses
published_requirement_narratives.text: NOTE: All courses must be taken for a letter grade.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: NIH Requirement

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Concentration Requirements

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Health Economics

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Thesis Units

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Pre-approved Electives
published_requirement_narratives.text: Other electives, consistent with the student’s development plan, may be approved by the student’s faculty advisor and the program director.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Proposal / Plan Requirements
published_requirement_narratives.text: Master's Program Proposal : Students must submit a Course Plan (Master's Program Proposal), approved by the primary advisor and program director, by the end of the autumn quarter of the first year. Thesis Proposal: Each student will submit a thesis proposal by the end of the first year in the program. The proposal should describe the research project which will fulfill the requirement for the master’s thesis, including identifying the research question and describing the data sources and methods which will be used, and list a second reader. In the proposal, the student should identify the members of their thesis committee. The primary advisor, the second reader, and the program director must approve the proposal. Collaborative Master's Plan : Each student will submit a Collaborative Master's Plan by November 1st of their second year. This plan will require an initial independent assessment of the student’s goals for the program, their career plans and their readiness to complete the thesis. The student will then meet with their advisor to review the assessment, allowing them to add and adjust steps required to meet the goals and satisfy the requirements for completion of the program.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Master's Thesis Requirements
published_requirement_narratives.text: Thesis: The thesis may take one of several forms, such as: Original analysis of data, whether collected primarily for the thesis or as secondary data analysis A decision model or cost-effectiveness analysis A quantitative policy analysis The quality of the master’s thesis should be such that it can be converted into a manuscript for publication. Thesis Committee: Each student will propose a thesis committee, to be approved by the Program Director, comprised of at least two faculty members associated with the master’s degree program, one of whom must be a core faculty member, and the second must be either core or affiliated faculty. All committee members must read and approve the final thesis. Depending on the project topic, additional faculty members may serve as mentors either as committee members or in a less formal arrangement.

value.A3i6E: Stanford Immunology is home to faculty, students, postdocs, and staff who work together to carry out internationally recognized research in immunology. The long tradition of collaboration among the immunology laboratories at Stanford fosters productive interdisciplinary research, with an emphasis on the application of molecular approaches to problems in cellular, translational, and clinical immunology. Faculty research interests include both basic science research and bench-to-bedside approaches, as well as computational and systems immunology. Graduate students and postdoctoral scholars receive high caliber, state-of-the art training through their participation in research, teaching, seminars, journal clubs, and the annual Stanford Immunology Scientific Conference.
value.ItCSB: The MS in Immunology aims to develop investigators with a strong foundation in immunology and related sciences to carry out innovative research: Acquire a fundamental, broad, and comprehensive body of knowledge and skills through an extensive curriculum Identify critical scientific questions, design, and conduct experiments using the most appropriate methods Read and critically analyze current literature in immunology and other relevant fields Present research findings and communicate ideas effectively to a variety of audiences Prepare manuscripts that will be published in leading journals Learn to teach effectively
value.advisingExpectations: The Immunology Program is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. This includes first-year advising by the program director and ongoing advising with the research mentor in subsequent years. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. The Individual Development Plan (IDP) must be completed by the advisor and advisee annually and entails an extensive interactive written and personal assessment of trainee goals, accomplishments, coursework, and areas for development. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. In addition, the advising process includes guidelines and expectations for graduate student professional conduct, which prepares the student to be responsible members of professional communities. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

Drawing on concepts, techniques and principles from multiple fields, such as biophysics, computational biology, synthetic biology, genetics, and structural biology, we develop a next generation of scientists skilled in interdisciplinary research, working in teams, mentoring, and communication.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Requirements Overview
published_requirement_narratives.text: Candidates for M.S. degrees at Stanford must satisfactorily complete a program of study that includes 45 units of graduate course work and research. Courses taken to meet program requirements must be taken for a letter grade and students must earn a minimum grade of at least a 'B' in every individual course. Students must also maintain a minimum GPA of 3.0 by University policy. Failure to maintain the required grades and grade point average is taken as evidence of unsatisfactory progress in the program. Students should complete their required courses within the first two years of study. Exceptions may be made in cases where it was impossible to schedule courses because they were not offered within a student’s first two years. Students may petition the MCP graduate committee for variances in the specific courses required, and such petitions may be granted in special circumstances, in cases where a student’s progress is otherwise exemplary.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Molecular Biology
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students should have basic competency in molecular biology. This requirement can be met based on undergrad curriculum/research. If not met, then the Stanford undergrad course BIO 83 can be taken to meet the requirement, but the units will not be applied toward the 45-unit minimum for the MS.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Electives
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students should complete the equivalent of 2 elective courses. Of the elective course options listed below, BIOC 241 and MCP 222 are considered 'full-value' courses, where each counts as 1 course. The other elective course options ( BIOS 202, BIOS 294, NEPR 201, and NEPR 204) are considered 'mini-courses,' and each counts as half (½) a course. 2 minicourses count as 1 'full-value' course. Student can choose from one of the three sets of options below to complete the Electives requirement.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Advanced Graduate Courses or Minicourses
published_requirement_narratives.text: Advanced graduate courses or minicourses for a minimum of 6 units total. These courses do not need to be MCP courses but must be in a relevant scientific topic and approved by the Director of Graduate Studies.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Laboratory Rotations
published_requirement_narratives.text: In addition to the course requirements detailed above, a student is expected to complete laboratory rotations during the first year - completing MCP 299, or an equivalent course. While students typically explore three rotations, a student may opt to do a greater number of shorter rotations, as long as the rotation process is completed by May 15 of the first academic year of study. The first two of these rotations must be in a laboratory within the Department, while subsequent rotations may be in any laboratory within the Stanford Biosciences Program. The first rotation should last 8 to 10 weeks and each subsequent rotation shall last no longer than 8 weeks. Shorter rotations are encouraged, as long as the total length of the rotations is between 20 and 26 weeks. MCP requires a lab rotation evaluation to be completed by faculty member and student at the end of the rotation. Continuation of rotations beyond May 15 will require the approval of the Director of Graduate Studies. Additional rotations and/or time for rotations will be considered in special circumstances, but in all cases, students should plan to join a dissertation lab no later than the beginning of Fall Quarter of the second year.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Written Portion of the Qualifying Exam
published_requirement_narratives.text: All students in the program must pass a qualifying examination to advance to candidacy for the Ph.D., or to earn the M.S. degree, if unable to complete the PhD. Students earning the M.S. degree instead of the PhD are required to complete the written section of the Qualifying Exam. It is expected that students take the qualifying examination by the end of the Autumn Quarter in the second year of study. Failure to take the qualifying exam by the end of Autumn Quarter of the second year of study is taken as evidence of unsatisfactory progress in the program. In any case, where a student thinks they need additional time to schedule and take their exam, a request must be submitted in writing to the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) by November 15 of Autumn Quarter. The DGS may opt to grant additional time in compelling circumstances that do not indicate poor progress or may refer the matter to the graduate committee for further action. Students are given two chances to unconditionally pass the qualifying examination. Failure to achieve an unconditional pass of the qualifying examination by the end of the Spring Quarter of the second year is grounds for dismissal from the program. Students form a qualifying examination committee consisting of at least 3 faculty members (members of the academic council, including the dissertation advisor), at least one of whom must be a member of MCP. This committee should be formed by the end of Spring Quarter of the first year of study. The composition of this committee should be approved by the Director of Graduate Studies. Students should also check with the department's student services office to make sure to file all required paperwork by the end of Spring Quarter. The University maintains certain deadlines for filing for candidacy, and it is the student’s responsibility to be aware of these deadlines.

value.A3i6E: The Master of Science (MS) in Laboratory Animal Science (MLAS) program in the Department of Comparative Medicine is a two-year graduate degree designed to prepare students for advanced careers in laboratory animal science, biomedical research, and related scientific fields. The curriculum provides comprehensive training in animal modeling and biomethodology, laboratory animal science, regulatory compliance, animal husbandry and welfare, organizational management, and research facility design. Students gain a strong academic foundation through interdisciplinary coursework while developing the technical, analytical, and professional skills needed to contribute to the advancement of biomedical research. Graduates are well prepared for careers in academia, biotechnology, pharmaceutical and biomedical industries, and research institutions, or for continued education in medical, veterinary, or other advanced graduate programs. Advanced Hands-On Learning in Biomedical Research The MLAS program emphasizes experiential learning by integrating classroom instruction with practical hands-on experiences. Students work alongside leading faculty, researchers, and senior staff, applying scientific principles in real-world laboratory settings while developing critical thinking, problem-solving, and research skills. NEW FOR 2027: Two Program Pathways Beginning with the 2027 cohort, the MLAS program offers two distinct academic pathways: a thesis track and a non-thesis track. This allows students to select the experience that best aligns with their career goals and professional interests. Thesis Track The traditional Thesis Track is designed for students seeking an in-depth research experience. Students are matched with a faculty mentor at the beginning of the program and remain in that laboratory throughout their degree. Working closely with their mentor, students develop and execute an independent research project that culminates in the completion and defense of a master's thesis. This pathway is ideal for students interested in research-intensive careers or pursuing advanced graduate degrees. Non-Thesis Track The Non-Thesis Track provides a broader experiential learning model for students interested in exploring multiple areas of laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Rather than completing a single, long-term research project, students participate in a series of quarter-long applied projects across a variety of disciplines and settings. Projects may be completed within Stanford laboratories as well as with partnering organizations, providing exposure to diverse research environments, technologies, and professional opportunities. This pathway emphasizes practical experience, professional development, and workforce readiness for careers across academia, industry, and research support organizations. It is ideal for students interested in pursuing advanced professional degrees (including veterinary and medical education and training) or who are exploring careers in research support areas such as regulatory compliance, biomedical research facility operations and management, animal husbandry and welfare, and investigator education and training. Applicants must indicate their preferred pathway—Thesis Track or Non-Thesis Track—at the time of application.
value.ItCSB: The Master of Science in Laboratory Animal Science (MLAS) program equips students with the scientific knowledge, technical expertise, and professional competencies needed to excel in laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Through rigorous coursework, hands-on learning, and individualized training, students develop a strong foundation in animal modeling and biomethodology, laboratory animal science, regulatory compliance, animal welfare, and research methodologies. Graduates are prepared to: Apply scientific principles and best practices in laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Design, conduct, and evaluate research using ethical and scientifically rigorous methodologies. Demonstrate knowledge of animal welfare, regulatory compliance, and responsible research practices. Communicate scientific findings effectively through written, oral, and professional presentations. Collaborate effectively in interdisciplinary research and laboratory environments. Apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills to address complex challenges in biomedical research. Students may tailor their educational experience by selecting either the Thesis Track , which emphasizes independent research under the guidance of a faculty mentor, or the Non-Thesis Track , which provides hands-on experience through a series of applied projects across diverse research settings. Both pathways prepare graduates for careers in academia, biotechnology, pharmaceutical and biomedical industries, and research institutions, as well as for advanced study in medical, veterinary, or graduate programs.
value.advisingExpectations: Academic Advising The MLAS program is committed to providing a collaborative and supportive advising experience that fosters academic achievement, professional growth, and career development. Upon admission, students are paired with advisors based on their selected program pathway. Thesis Track : Students are matched with a faculty advisor whose research interests align with their academic and professional goals. This faculty mentor serves as the student's primary research advisor throughout the program, providing guidance on research design, thesis development, academic planning, and career preparation. Non-Thesis Track : Students are advised by the Student Services Officer, Program Director, and designated program faculty, who provide guidance on academic planning, professional development, and the successful completion of quarter-long applied projects. Students may also work with project supervisors at Stanford or partnering organizations during individual project rotations. All students are required to meet with Faculty advisors and Student Services Officer at least once each quarter to review academic progress, discuss professional goals, and support the development of the student's Individual Development Plan (IDP). Students and advisors are encouraged to meet regularly throughout the year to discuss coursework, research or project experiences, career exploration, and professional development opportunities. Successful advising is a shared responsibility. Students are expected to actively engage in the advising relationship by seeking guidance, communicating regularly with their advisor or mentor, and maintaining familiarity with program policies, degree requirements, and academic milestones. To foster a productive mentoring relationship, students and advisors should periodically review expectations and maintain open, respectful, and professional communication. The Student Services Officer monitors each student's academic progress and the completion of program requirements. Detailed information regarding degree requirements, academic milestones, and advising expectations is available throughout the program website and MLAS Handbook In addition to faculty mentorship, students are encouraged to work closely with the department's Student Services Officer, who can connect them with Stanford resources that support academic success, career planning, health and wellness, and professional development. Additionally, the program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE), at Graduate Academic Policies (GAP), and at Graduate Advising . For more information regarding Graduate Student Advising and Postdoctoral/Resident Mentoring, contact the following people: Graduate Student Advising: Venessa Juarez (Student Services Officer), venessaj@stanford.edu Program Director: Megan Albertelli (Comparative Medicine Chair), megan.albertelli@stanford.edu Program Co-Director: Jose Vilches-Moure, jvilches@stanford.edu Postdoctoral Student/Residents: David Bentzel (Laboratory Animal Medicine Residency Director), dbentzel@stanford.edu Postdoctoral/Resident: Katherine Gates (Resident and Trainee Wellness Advisor), kvgates@stanford.edu

published_requirement_narratives.text: Requirements for all students: All courses must be taken at the 100 level or above 36 of 45 units must be 200-level or above All graded courses must achieve a grade of C or higher Adhere to the university minimum for an overall GPA (3.0) CompMed 205, 210, 211, 290, and 291 MUST be taken for a letter grade Students must complete at least 45 units of academic work. All required courses must be completed and will count toward the 45-unit minimum. Thesis Track: The remaining units needed to meet the 45-unit minimum can be fulfilled with research credit (COMPMED 399 - Graduate research) or electives, as approved by each student’s research mentor. Non Thesis Track: In addition to the required courses (listed below), students should enroll in COMPMED 260 for rotation credit. Out-of-department electives should be approved by the department's Student Services Officer before enrolling. Students will also participate in 3-4 quarters of hands-on rotations, for credit. Hands-on rotations will be done both within and outside of Stanford University. Instead of a final thesis, trainees in the non-thesis track will produce deliverables for each rotation, including (but not limited to) generation of standard operating procedures (SOP), reports on findings, recommendations and implementation guidelines, educational modules, etc. The type of deliverable for each rotation will be determined by each rotation mentor(s).

Students must present their research to the department. While not required, students are encouraged to publish a research paper that would meet the thesis requirement. Non Thesis Option: Hands-on rotations will be done both within and outside of Stanford University. Instead of a final thesis, trainees in the non-thesis track will produce deliverables for each rotation, including (but not limited to) generation of standard operating procedures (SOP), reports on findings, recommendations and implementation guidelines, educational modules, etc.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Advanced Courses
published_requirement_narratives.text: ​​Our program embraces the highly interdisciplinary nature of neuroscience research by allowing students to create an individualized curriculum of advanced topic courses best suited to their research agenda and scientific development needs. This approach has empowered students to take advantage of the breadth of expertise across the university. A minimum of six credits of Advanced Topics coursework is required of each student. Students select the courses while meeting the following criteria: (1) at least one course must be taken with a minimum of three units, (2) the course must have a clear means of evaluation (i.e., problem sets, paper writing, class presentations), and (3) the student must detail how the course relates to the student’s project or domain of neuroscience. This information is submitted in writing along with the course syllabus and examples of problem sets to the co-directors/curriculum committee co-chairs for approval. Six units of advanced neuroscience coursework are required. To complete the six units, at least one course must be three units or more; the remaining units can be completed with a combination of smaller-unit courses (e.g., 3+2+1, 3+2+2, 4+2). Pre-approval for advanced courses is required. Required courses must be taken for a letter grade and passed with a 3.0 (B) or better.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Master's Thesis Defense
published_requirement_narratives.text: MS Students will write a proposal in the style of an NIH NRSA proposal and a written rigor document which outlines how the proposed research has addressed NIH's four key areas of rigor as well as a plan for dissemination for research outcomes and products. The student will defend the proposal and rigor document by oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee. The student will complete the proposed Master's thesis project and defend the project through an oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee. The student must defend the thesis project through oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee by the end of the 2nd year.

value.A3i6E: This program is only open to existing students in the STMRM-PHD Program.
value.ItCSB: The SCBRM program encourages students to complete all Ph.D. requirements by their 5th or 6th year. In some cases, it may be necessary and/or advised for a student to graduate with an M.Sc . (Master of Science) instead of a Ph.D. Students who fail to advance to candidacy, or Ph.D. candidates who have displayed insufficient progress for more than two quarters (e.g., received two N- grades), may graduate with an M.Sc . degree. Students wishing to do so must have completed 45 academic units of study and submit a scholarly 20-page research report (standard NIH format). This report must meet a sufficient scholarly standard as judged by the Director of Graduate Studies. A SCBRM Ph.D. student who has passed the qualifying exam and is in good standing will generally not pursue an M.Sc . degree. However, if extenuating circumstances arise, and are approved by the SCBRM Director of Graduate Studies, a Ph.D. candidate may exit the program with an M.Sc . by completing the same requirements.
value.advisingExpectations: The Program in Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine is committed to providing academic advising to support graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.
value.programGradingPolicies: All required courses, including those counting toward the 10 units of elective credit, must be taken for a letter grade if offered and must be passed with a B grade or better. The course must be repeated if a student does not earn a B grade or better.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Requirements Overview
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students in the PhD program may apply for an MS degree after satisfactorily completing the course and laboratory requirements of the first two years, including the qualifying exam. Postdoctoral research training is available to graduates having a PhD or MD degree. To meet theses requirements, each student must complete three one-quarter laboratory rotations during the first year. All rotations must be approved by the DGS, Executive Director and SSO prior to the start of the rotation. Two rotations (including the first rotation) must be done with ISCBRM faculty. Students may complete one of the rotations with a faculty member who is Academic Council (AC) outside the program with program approval (by DGS and Executive Director). Students must choose a dissertation advisor before the end of summer quarter of the first year. SCBRM graduate students must be registered in all quarters. All required courses, including those counting toward the 10 units of elective credit, must be taken for a letter grade if offered and must be passed with a B grade or better. The course must be repeated if a student does not earn a B grade or better.

value.A3i6E: Master’s in Translational Medicine (M-TRAM) is a professional degree program that trains students to advance promising biomedical solutions from early-stage research to full regulatory approval. Technology focus areas include immunotherapy, gene therapy, vaccines, biomarkers, single-cell omics, and medical devices. M-TRAM combines flexible classroom learning with hands-on, team-based medical research, one-on-one mentoring by renowned Stanford faculty and investigators, and on-site biotechnology training. M-TRAM focuses on three integrated areas representing key stages of translational medicine. Rather than specializing in only one area, students develop strong working knowledge across all three domains throughout the program: Early Translation: Basic Science to Preclinical Clinical Translation: Clinical Investigation Late Translation: Medical Adoption and Commercialization There are two complementary M-TRAM Tracks based on the type of capstone project students pursue: TRIP (Translational Research Individual Project) : track requiring a faculty-mentored individual capstone research project . TEAM (Translation, Entrepreneurship, and Applied Medicine Project) : track requiring a collaborative team-based capstone project , organized by therapeutic or focus area. TRIP and TEAM track students have overlapping but separate coursework requirements, as indicated here: https://med.stanford.edu/m-tram/academics/schedules.html

value.ItCSB: By the end of the one-year program, students will have gained the problem-solving skills, competencies, and strategies: Expand professional networks and career opportunities Develop a complete product development plan encompassing pre-clinical, clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory modules Identify unmet medical needs Develop scientific hypotheses Design clinical studies Apply clinical specimens to emerging technologies Understand research design, methodology, data analysis, data reporting

value.description: The Biomedical Physics PhD program aims to offer unique interdisciplinary training in physics and engineering applied to solve clinical problems. This burgeoning translational field integrates topics including medical physics, diagnostic imaging, and molecular imaging and diagnostics. Synergistic with multiple departments and institutes from the School of Medicine, Engineering, and Humanities and Sciences, the BMP program leverages Stanford’s outstanding faculty, research, and resources to create a world-class training program. It targets physics, bioscience, and engineering students seeking to become the next generation of leaders focused on addressing the technical challenges of clinical medicine.

value.description: Biochemistry is a department within the School of Medicine, with offices and labs in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine at the Stanford Medical Center, the Shriram Center for Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering, and the Stanford Genome Technology Center. Undergraduates and graduate and medical school students may take courses the department offers. The Department of Biochemistry focuses on the molecular basis of life by studying the structures and functions of proteins and nucleic acids, the control of development, molecular motors and the cytoskeleton, trafficking of proteins between organelles, regulation of gene expression, protein homeostasis, structure and design, genetic and epigenetic control of chromosome function, and the application of genomics, all toward the understanding of health and disease. Advanced courses in more specialized areas emphasize the most recent developments in biochemistry, biophysics, cell biology, and molecular biology. These courses include the physical chemistry of proteins and nucleic acids, membrane biology and biochemistry, the cytoskeleton, mechanisms and regulation of nucleic acid replication and recombination, the biochemistry of bacterial and animal viruses, the molecular basis of morphogenesis, and the structure and function of both eukaryotic and prokaryotic chromosomes. The Department of Biochemistry offers a PhD program that begins in Autumn quarter of each year. The program of study is designed to prepare students for productive careers in biochemistry; its emphasis is training in research, and each student works closely with faculty members. Opportunities exist for directed reading and research in biochemistry and molecular biology using the most advanced research facilities, including those for light and electron microscopy, chromatography and electrophoresis, protein and nucleic acid purification, rapid kinetic analysis, synthesis and analysis, single-molecule analyses using laser light traps, microarray generation and analysis, and computer graphic workstation facilities for protein and nucleic acid structural analysis. Ongoing research uses a variety of organisms, from bacteria to animal cells.

value.description: The Cancer Biology PhD program was established in 1978 at Stanford University. During the past four decades, the understanding of cancer has increased dramatically with the discovery of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, DNA damage and repair pathways, cell cycle regulation, angiogenesis and responses to hypoxia, and the molecular basis of metastasis, among others. In addition, parallel analysis methods, including genomic and proteomic approaches, have begun to refine and redefine the taxonomy of cancer diagnosis. This explosion of basic and clinical science has, in turn, resulted in the first successful cancer chemotherapies and immunotherapies based on knowledge of specific molecular targets. Stanford presents a unique environment to pursue interdisciplinary cancer research because the School of Medicine, the School of Humanities and Sciences, and the School of Engineering are located on a single campus, all within walking distance of one another. Our students are not limited to a single department in choosing their research advisors. The Cancer Biology PhD program currently has approximately 65 graduate students in various basic science and clinical departments throughout the School of Medicine and School of Humanities and Sciences. A training grant from the National Cancer Institute, a branch of the United States government, supports many students. The Cancer Biology PhD program is committed to fostering a diverse community of students. The program welcomes all individuals and strives to support them so they achieve their full potential. It values the diversity of its students because culture, socioeconomic and educational background, race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, physical ability, life experiences, hobbies, and interests allow the program as a group to reach a greater level of innovation in cancer research.

value.description: The Biomedical Data Science Program is interdisciplinary and offers instruction and research opportunities leading to MS and PhD degrees in Biomedical Data Science. The program emphasizes research to develop novel computational methods that can advance biomedicine. Students receive training in investigating new approaches to conceptual modeling and developing new algorithms that address challenging problems in the biological sciences and clinical medicine.

value.description: The Department of Chemical and Systems Biology offers interdisciplinary training to prepare students for independent careers in biomedical science. The program’s primary focus is cell signaling, chemical biology, and systems biology. The program leading to the PhD degree includes formal and informal study in chemical biology, systems biology, drug discovery, biochemistry, and other areas of relevance to the interests of particular students. First-year students spend one quarter in each of three different laboratories, working closely with other graduate students, a professor, and postdoctoral fellows on various research projects. During the fourth quarter, the student chooses a faculty mentor — based on available positions and the student’s interest — with whom to undertake thesis research. During or before the eighth quarter of study, students must pass a qualifying exam which consists of an oral exam on general knowledge and defense of a research proposal. Course requirements are fulfilled during the first two years of study; the later years of the four- to six-year program are devoted to full-time dissertation research. Close tutorial contact between students and faculty is stressed throughout the program. Research opportunities also exist for medical students and undergraduates. The limited size of the labs in the department allows for close tutorial contact between students, postdoctoral fellows, and faculty. The department participates in the four-quarter Health and Human Disease and Practice of Medicine sequence, providing medical students with a comprehensive, systems-based education in physiology, pathology, microbiology, and pharmacology.

value.description: A fundamental problem in biology is how the complex set of multicellular structures that characterize an adult animal is generated from the fertilized egg. Recent advances at the molecular level, particularly concerning the genetic control of development, have been explosive. These advances represent the beginning of a significant movement in the biological sciences toward understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying developmental decisions and the resulting morphogenetic processes. This new thrust in developmental biology derives from the extraordinary methodological advances of the past decade in molecular genetics, immunology, and biochemistry. However, it also derives from groundwork from classical developmental studies, the rapid advances in cell biology and animal virology, and models borrowed from prokaryotic systems. The work is increasingly related to human diseases, including oncogene function and inherited genetic disease. The department is located in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine within the Stanford University Medical Center.

The program trains students in the tools of modern epidemiology, with heavy emphasis on statistics, causal inference, computer science, genetics, genomics, and informatics. We welcome applicants with diverse backgrounds.

value.description: Health Policy investigates how social factors, financing systems, organizational structures and processes, health technologies, and personal behaviors affect the accessibility, quality, and cost of health care and, ultimately, our health and well-being. Stanford Health Policy offers a PhD program that promises to educate students who will be scholarly leaders in the field of health policy and will be highly knowledgeable about the theoretical and empirical approaches that can be applied in the development of improvements in health policy and the health care system. The curriculum offers courses across a wide range of health policy areas, including health economics, health insurance and government program operation, health financing, international health policy and economic development, cost-effectiveness analysis and the evaluation of new technologies, health law and ethics, health systems operations, relevant statistical and methodological approaches, and health policy issues related to public health concerns like obesity and chronic disease. See the program’s website for additional program information, including (but not limited to) faculty lists, admissions information, and deadlines. Address admission inquiries to the Health Policy Admissions Team at hrpadmissions@stanford.edu . Applications to the program must be submitted through the Stanford Graduate Admissions website by clicking Apply Now.

value.description: The Immunology doctoral program offers instruction and research opportunities leading to a PhD in Immunology. Two tracks are offered: Track 1: Molecular, Cellular, and Translational Immunology Track 2: Computational and Systems Immunology Molecular, Cellular, and Translational Immunology The MCTI track comprises interdisciplinary research that emphasizes the application of molecular approaches to open questions in cellular and clinical immunology. Graduate students in this track gain an advanced understanding of basic molecular and cellular biology, biochemistry, genetics, and cellular signaling concepts and experimental techniques and apply this knowledge to immunology problems. MCTI faculty interests include both bench-to-bedside approaches and basic science research. Computational & Systems Immunology The past decade has seen an explosion in the availability of high-throughput datasets spanning information on everything from DNA sequences to RNA transcript abundances, single-cell protein profiles, protein variants and metabolite profiles. These multi-dimensional omics datasets are complex to integrate, visualize and analyze for those not well versed in systems biology and bioinformatics. A new generation of scientists is needed to take advantage of these resources to ask and answer novel important questions in immunology. The CSI track will generate a class of hybrid scientists to identify important problems in immunology and to devise appropriate integrated computational/experimental plans for tackling them.

value.description: The University requirements for the MS are described in the " Graduate Degrees " section of this bulletin. The Department of Genetics offers an MS in Human Genetics and Genetic Counseling, which is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Genetic Counseling. This program prepares students to practice in the healthcare profession of genetic counseling. The program is a full time two-year program, and accepts students to begin the program only in autumn quarter. Students must be admitted directly into this program and cannot automatically transfer from the PhD programs within the department, or vice versa. While courses are oriented primarily towards genetic counseling students, some courses may also be taken by medical students, other graduate students, residents, or post-doctoral fellows, and (with permission) undergraduates.

value.description: The Department of Molecular and Cellular Physiology is located in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine. A central goal of physiology in the post-genomic era is to understand how thousands of encoded proteins serve to bring about the highly coordinated behavior of cells and tissues. Research in the department approaches this goal at many levels of organization, ranging from single molecules and individual cells to multicellular systems and the whole organism. The faculty share common interests in the molecular mechanisms of cell signaling and behavior, with a special focus on structure/function analysis of ion channels and G-protein coupled receptors, and their roles at the cellular, organ, and whole-organism levels; the molecular basis of sensory transduction, synaptic transmission, plasticity and memory; the role of ion channels and calcium in controlling gene expression in neural and immune cells; and the regulation of vesicle trafficking and targeting, cell polarity, and cell-cell interactions in the nervous system and in epithelia. Research programs employ a wide range of approaches, including molecular and cell biology, biochemistry, genetics, biophysics, x-ray crystallography, and solution NMR, electrophysiology, and in vitro and in vivo imaging with confocal and multi-photon microscopy.

value.description: The graduate program in Structural Biology is intended to prepare students for careers as independent investigators in cell and molecular biology. The principal requirement of a PhD degree is the completion of research constituting an original and significant contribution to advancing knowledge. It is training in a major with connections to biophysics (e.g., physics, chemistry, or biology, with a quantitative background equivalent to that of an undergraduate physics or chemistry major at Stanford). Current research topics in the department lie in gene expression; theoretical, crystallographic, and genetic analysis of protein structure; and cell-cell interaction. See Stanford’s School of Medicine website for further information. Admission Applicants to the program should have a bachelor’s degree and complete at least a year of coursework in biology, mathematics, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, and physics. The department must receive applications before December 15 for notification by April 15. Application to the National Science Foundation for fellowship support is also encouraged. Prospective applicants should contact the Department of Structural Biology for further information. The GRE general score is optional, and the GRE subject score is not required. It is recommended that prospective applicants have completed the following courses (or their equivalent) before applying: UNITS course Organic Polyfunctional Compounds 3 course Foundations of Physical Chemistry 4 course Physical Chemistry II 3 course Physical Chemistry III 3 course Applied Biochemistry 2

value.description: The Stanford Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine (SCBRM) program is dedicated to doctoral education that translates basic science to clinical applications, typically called Translational Science, and is of intense interest internationally in medical schools and universities. Our doctoral program provides exceptional didactic education and research experience in the basic sciences underlying stem cell biology. In addition, program participants will receive specialized training in developing and clinically applying discoveries in the basic sciences to achieve regenerative therapies. Thus, our graduates will be uniquely positioned to develop successful translational careers in Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine. They will emerge prepared to deliver on their passion for improving the human condition. The core curriculum combines unique research and clinical/professional immersion rotations to provide opportunities for doctoral students to specialize in the broad subject of translational medicine and yet focus specifically on the fundamentals of SCBRM. The curriculum combines genetics and developmental biology education with an introductory laboratory-based stem cell course, an advanced course in stem cell biology and regenerative medicine, and a clinical rotation with alternative law, business, and/or engineering opportunities.

facts.value: MBA applicants require U.S. bachelor degree or equivalent (including eligible international three-year degrees); no minimum GPA. All applicants submit GMAT or GRE (no minimum, no superscore, only one test sitting reported); Executive Assessment not accepted. For 2026-27, scores expiring before Jun 1, 2027 should be officially reported at application submission and may arrive after deadline. English test (TOEFL, IELTS Academic or PTE Academic) is required if undergraduate classes were not all taught exclusively in English, unless later graduate program was exclusively English; citizenship/work experience do not exempt. Minimums: TOEFL 100 before Jan 21 2026 or 5.0 on/after, IELTS 7.0, PTE 68; scores valid two years and test must precede round deadline. Application includes education/transcripts, personal/activities/awards, professional experience and resume, two recommendations (preferably supervisors), essays, optional short answer, fee. Unofficial transcripts at application, official after admission. Application decisions are holistic; calculus/statistics/microeconomics strengthen readiness but are not formal prerequisites.

English scores expire after two years and must be valid on round deadline.

facts.value: MSx is a 12-month full-time in-person Stanford GSB MS in Management. Applicants require a U.S. bachelor’s degree or equivalent (international three-year degrees included); only rare exceptions are considered. At least eight years of post-graduate professional work experience is required; managerial experience is valued but not required. No minimum GPA; application requires education history/transcripts, test score, professional history/resume (maximum two pages), two recommendations, essays and fee. GMAT, GRE or Executive Assessment is required before application with no test waivers; LSAT/MCAT are not substitutes. TOEFL/PTE/IELTS is required if English was not the primary language of instruction or any classes used another language; online PTE not accepted. Applicants report only one testing session if repeated; online GMAT/GRE/EA/TOEFL/IELTS accepted. 2026-27 rounds: Oct 8 2026, Jan 6 2027 (MBA/MSx joint), and Feb 11 2027, all 4 p.m. Pacific; decisions Dec 9 2026 or Apr 1 2027. Nonrefundable fee USD 275. A 12-month 2026-27 cost estimate is USD 221,190 single / USD 258,342 married, including tuition USD 154,828. Need-based fellowships and loans are available to admitted students regardless of citizenship; admissions decisions precede aid application.
conditions: MSx has no test waivers. Valid test score is required to receive an interview invitation.
English test is required under either language-of-instruction condition; no general nationality-based exemption is stated in the reviewed page.
Cost is for the 12-month period July 2026 to June 2027 and includes insurance even if alternative coverage exists.
exceptions: Joint applicants need GMAT or GRE because the MBA does not accept EA.
Applicants may apply once per application year. Deferral is considered only in rare extraordinary circumstances.
Need-based funding is decided only for admitted students and is available regardless of citizenship.

facts.value: GSB PhD applicants must hold, or expect before enrollment, a U.S. bachelor's degree or recognized international equivalent. A complete application includes a statement of purpose, CV, three references, GRE, TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic if applicable, uploaded official transcripts, online submission, and a USD 125 application fee. No minimum GPA, GRE score, particular prior field, work experience, or MBA/graduate degree is required. Applicants may also apply to another Stanford program. All applicants must submit GRE scores, including every administration from Dec 1, 2021 through Dec 1, 2026 for Fall 2027; GRE At Home is accepted. Self-reported and official GRE scores are required, but self-reported scores suffice for initial review while official results are pending; do not superscore. Official GRE scores go to ETS code 4704. Applicants without an English-test exemption must submit TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic; minimums are TOEFL 100 for tests before Jan 21, 2026, TOEFL 5 for tests on/after that date, or IELTS 7. For Autumn 2027, English test dates must fall from Dec 1, 2024 through Dec 1, 2026. TOEFL MyBest scores are accepted; IELTS superscores are not. Official English scores are required, with self-reporting sufficient for initial review while official scores are pending.
conditions: International degree equivalence may be checked with WES; this is a recommendation, not a Stanford credential evaluation.
Field choice determines research area and related preparation.
English-test exemption may require supporting documentation as a condition of admission.
Admitted students accepting an offer must take the Stanford English Placement Test if their application TOEFL was below 109 or IELTS below 8.
exceptions: English scores are not required at application if the applicant is a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, has English as a first language, earned a U.S. bachelor, master, or doctoral degree (or international equivalent) at a university where all instruction was in English, or has at least two consecutive years of professional or educational experience in English within the past 10 years.

facts.value: GSB PhD is one Business Administration PhD award with seven fields of study: Accounting; Economic Analysis & Policy; Finance; Marketing; Operations, Information & Technology; Organizational Behavior; and Political Economics. The program is five to six years full time in Stanford, California. Incoming doctoral students receive a financial fellowship covering tuition, living stipend, and health fees for five years, conditional on satisfactory academic progress and program milestones, with a possible sixth-year extension. Incoming students in 2026-27 receive a living stipend of USD 59,500 annually. Research and course assistantships are typically included in the support package; professional development grants cover eligible conference travel, publication submissions, and professional organization fees.
conditions: The USD 59,500 stipend is an annual 2026-27 incoming-student amount, not a Fall 2027 award quote.
Five-year support depends on satisfactory academic progress and program milestones; a sixth year is possible rather than automatic.
The reviewed financial-aid page does not specify a separate summer stipend amount or payment schedule.

facts.value: For Fall 2027, a bachelor degree or equivalent must be completed or expected by Summer 2027; all offers are conditional on graduation. LSAC application opens Sep 15, 2026 and is due Feb 15, 2027 11:59 p.m. PT; KHS files must be complete Dec 1, 2026. Required: 1-2 page resume, roughly two-page personal statement, required viewpoint essay (1-2 pages), 250-word answer to one of three prompts, 2-4 LSAC letters, CAS transcript report, LSAT or GRE. Valid LSAT scores must all be reported; score dates before June 2021 invalid, Argumentative Writing required, latest LSAT Jan 2027. GRE-only route permitted; GRE scores before June 2021 invalid, all valid scores submitted, suggested test by Feb 1 2027. Fee USD 85; SLS fee waiver must be requested before application, with 5-7 business days processing. No admissions interviews. Rolling decisions (accept/reject/waitlist), first response target Apr 30. Deposit secures enrollment; limited one-year deferral requires nonrefundable tuition deposit; waitlist admits cannot defer. SLS may withdraw offers for significant performance decline, misrepresentation, serious integrity concerns, or another law-school enrollment commitment/deposit.
conditions: All application items are applicant responsibility; file is complete only when required records arrive.
Fee waiver request must precede LSAC submission; current fee-waiver instruction page gives 5-7 business day processing.
exceptions: If an applicant has any valid LSAT, it must be reported; GRE-only applicants may omit LSAT.
Admissions Committee does not interview applicants.
Waitlist admits cannot defer.

facts.value: Four LLM specializations: Corporate Governance & Practice, Environmental Law & Policy, International Economic Law, Business and Policy, and Law, Science & Technology; primary law degree must be earned outside U.S. SPILS is a research-oriented route for foreign-law-degree holders; the JSM is awarded through SPILS and requires JD/equivalent plus participation. LLM and SPILS have separate admissions decisions. JSD applicants have two routes: Stanford SPILS graduates and students from Stanford/other U.S. law schools who complete an LLM before JSD; LLM-route applicants submit serious independent original research. Neither SPILS nor Stanford LLM admission guarantees JSD. MLS is a nonprofessional degree for a small number of advanced graduate students/scholars without legal training; Bulletin inventory confirms it is not coterm.
conditions: LLM and SPILS admit small cohorts; MLS admits very few if any.
JSD antecedent route must be complete before starting the JSD; application is a separate selection decision.
exceptions: Current JSD program page resolves the initial ambiguity: U.S.-based law-school LLM applicants are also a stated route, alongside SPILS completers.
MLS is not a coterm degree.

facts.value: LLM/SPILS Fall 2027 applications open Sep 15, 2026 and are due Dec 1, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. PT; KHS file-complete deadline is same date. JSD application opens Feb 2027 and deadline is Apr 2027, both officially TBA. Advanced app fee USD 85 per program; separate fee for each program. Shared LSAC application materials: 1-2 page resume, 2-3 page personal statement, two recommendation letters, official transcripts, TOEFL; SPILS/JSD add research proposal and third letter; JSD also requires 1-2 examples of English scholarly writing. LSAC CAS and recommendation service required; direct submissions rejected. TOEFL iBT minimum is 100 before Jan 21, 2026; for tests on/after that date, overall 5.5 with reading/listening at least 5.5 and writing/speaking at least 5.0. Scores to LSAC institution code 8395. Native-English applicants still request TOEFL waiver; full-time study/work in English for at least two years may qualify with formal request/evidence. LLM normally expects two years legal practice; waiver explanation possible. Decisions expected by mid-April 2027.
conditions: All required documents must arrive through LSAC services.
Applicants under two years legal practice need an unusual-circumstances waiver explanation for LLM.
English proficiency required; eligible waiver must be formally requested with proof.
exceptions: JSD application dates are TBA, and its KHS application must be submitted in a prior masters-application year.

facts.value: 2026-27 JD standard cost-of-attendance estimate is USD 125,124 on-campus or USD 126,216 off-campus for a single student; tuition is USD 79,779. Need-based aid uses FAFSA and CSS Profile and combines tuition fellowships, government/private loans; it is re-evaluated annually and level is not guaranteed for all three years. Stanford reports approximately 75-80% of students receive aid, with average fellowship portion USD 25,000-28,000 annually. Age-based parental contribution rules apply to CSS resource assessment. Yellow Ribbon is additional for eligible 100% Chapter 33 benefit recipients; LRAP is a post-JD loan assistance program for qualifying public-service employment.
conditions: Cost figures are standard single-student budget estimates; medical insurance is waivable and shown separately.
Need-based award depends on demonstrated need and annual review.
exceptions: Yellow Ribbon requires 100% Post-9/11 GI Bill eligibility; veteran benefits are not universal grants.
LRAP is post-graduation loan support, not tuition reduction at admission.

facts.value: For Fall 2027 MD admission, applicants need a recognized U.S. bachelor degree or equivalent; foreign bachelor degree holders may need WES equivalency and one in-person academic year at an accredited institution in the U.S., Canada, or U.K. Eligible groups include citizens, permanent residents, DACA, undocumented and visa-eligible international applicants; undocumented admits need legal status by matriculation. No required undergraduate courses; coursework areas are recommended. At least one MCAT after Jan 2023 and by Aug 22, 2026 is required. AMCAS due Oct 1, 2026 11:59 p.m. ET; invited applicants submit Stanford supplemental materials by Oct 9, 2026 11:59 p.m. PT. Three to six AMCAS letters, with at least three received by supplemental deadline; invitations to interview roll from August; decisions Jan-Mar; accept one offer by Apr 30. Fee is required but amount is not exposed; only AAMC Fee Assistance Program waiver approved before primary application is accepted. No Early Decision.
conditions: Timeline page does not identify its applicable entering class/cycle on the reviewed content; confirm before applying.
The 2026-entry how-to-apply page is historical and has not been used to set current MCAT dates.
exceptions: Supplemental application is by invitation after AMCAS receipt.

facts.value: Stanford MD Discovery Curriculum can be completed at different paces: pre-clerkship phase in two years or, after applying for the option, spread over three years. Students must pass USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK. 2026-27 regular MD tuition is USD 24,034 per quarter for Autumn, Winter, Spring, and Summer; research rate USD 3,993 per quarter applies under specified 100%-research/after-residency conditions. Insurance and mandatory fees may be additional.
conditions: Research tuition is conditional and not a general student rate.
Required tuition is quarter-based; annual total depends on enrollment status and additional fees.
exceptions: MD students enrolled in other Stanford degrees may be charged under separate rules.

facts.value: Current Stanford MD students may apply internally to MSTP, commonly after M1 or during M2/M2B, with later-stage cases discussed individually. They need good standing, a defined thesis and a committed adviser. Students outside Stanford MD and students enrolled in another institution's PhD are ineligible for this internal funding route. Current Stanford PhD students must be in good standing, have passed the qualifying exam, and apply to MD by fall of G3; MD admission is a separate decision. The published Autumn2026-27 funding deadline was January20,2026 at5p.m.Pacific and has passed. Materials include a cover page, statement of at most250words, mentor letter, access to the MD application, NIH biosketch, dual-degree form and research proposal. An oral presentation lasts10minutes followed by10minutes of questions. Funding start depends on availability, degree approvals and full-time thesis research.
conditions: The January20,2026 deadline does not establish the next internal funding cycle.
The internal admissions page restricts MSTP funding to US citizens and permanent residents.
exceptions: The internal application pathway is distinct from initial external MSTP/MD application.
Current Stanford PhD students have an eligibility path, but MD admission remains a separate decision.

facts.value: For the MSPA 2026-27 application timeline leading to August 2027 entry, CASPA opened Apr 30, 2026; the application had to be in Complete status in CASPA by Jul 15, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (deadline passed); interviews Autumn 2026 and orientation/classes begin Aug 2027. Only CASPA application status establishes deadline compliance; no other proof or evidence is accepted. Failure to maintain Complete status moving forward jeopardizes admission consideration. The only minimum admission requirement is a qualifying in-person U.S./Canada bachelor's degree or qualifying U.S. graduate degree by Jul 1 of the matriculation year (July 1, 2027 for August 2027 entry); no specific major. Foreign-degree-only applicants are ineligible, WES equivalency is not accepted, and no waiver applies. Recommended: GRE/MCAT/PA-CAT (PA-CAT preferred), preparatory coursework, 500+ clinical hours and three references. No minimum GPA or test score; one CASPA personal statement up to 5,000 characters. Three references recommended, max five; friends/family/healthcare providers excluded. About 10% interview. USD 1,000 nonrefundable seat deposit credited to first-quarter tuition; no advanced placement. Stanford undergraduate applicants may also apply as internal applicants through the same CASPA route; Stanford identifies no coterm degree or advanced placement for this program.
conditions: CASPA Complete status must be attained by the published deadline and maintained afterward; no other proof or evidence of completion is accepted, and processing extensions are not granted.
Test scores must be verified by the deadline to count; admitted applicants without PA-CAT may be required to complete it before enrollment, without affecting admission status.
exceptions: Tests, recommendations and preparatory coursework/experience are recommendations, not minimum admission conditions.
International applicants qualify only with the specified qualifying U.S./Canada degree; no degree waiver.
Internal Stanford undergraduate eligibility uses the same qualifying degree requirement and external CASPA application; no coterm route exists.

facts.value: For 2026-27 MSPA, standard tuition is USD 21,815 per quarter for nine quarters. Mandatory quarterly fees/books subtotal USD 850; disability insurance USD 40 annually. Cardinal Care is optional at USD 2,936 per quarter; private qualifying insurance may be used. Living estimates: USD 12,960 per quarter on campus, USD 14,435 off campus. Published total-program on-campus budget without Cardinal Care is USD 326,145 for AY 2026-27 matriculants, with future incremental tuition increases likely.
conditions: Standard progress assumes nine quarters; extra terms incur further charges.
Health insurance is mandatory but Cardinal Care is optional if qualifying private insurance is maintained.
exceptions: Housing and insurance choices change total attendance costs.

facts.value: MS in Medicine without subplan is reserved for MED-MD students. Berg Scholars Biomedical Investigation MS application is restricted to Stanford MD students approved for a split curriculum and at the end of the second year; approved off-cycle applications may be considered, but funding is not retroactive. Applicants should contact the program director early. Materials include a research proposal (maximum five pages), permission to access the AMCAS application, proposed mentor recommendation, brief career/coursework/committee/Gantt-chart statement, and oral presentation with Q&A. Application submission, review, interview, presentation and selection occur around the end of Summer Quarter after M2; decisions precede the next quarter. MS requires at least 45 unduplicated units (33 research and 12 coursework), completed within three years of the first graduate quarter while pursuing MD.
conditions: Applicants must be approved for split curriculum and be at end of M2.
Degree requirements must be completed within three years of first graduate quarter; MS and MD units cannot be duplicated toward residency.
exceptions: This is an internal additional award, not an open external MS admission route.
An approved off-cycle applicant may apply, but acceptance does not provide retroactive funding.

facts.value: The 12-month MSx program cost of attendance for July 2026-June 2027 is USD 221,190 for a single student and USD 258,342 for a married student; tuition is USD 154,828. Budget includes housing, living expenses, USD 250 documentation fee, medical insurance, health fee. Eligible child allowances are separately estimated. Need-based gap between attendance cost and expected student contribution is covered by a mix of fellowship and loans; fellowship is gift aid, based solely on demonstrated need, and is available regardless of citizenship.
conditions: Cost figures cover 12 months from July 2026 to June 2027; household costs differ.
Financial aid reviewed for admitted students after admission; need-based award is not an admission consideration.
exceptions: Applicants may receive fellowship and loan package regardless of citizenship.

facts.value: For Fall 2027 GSB PhD entry, the application portal sets the deadline at Dec 1, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time, including recommendation letters and other materials. Applications opened in early September 2026. Only applications complete by the deadline are guaranteed review. Admission decisions are typically available by mid-March and are sent by email. Admitted students are expected to enroll in September 2027; ordinarily they must reapply rather than defer.
conditions: The portal deadline applies to the GSB PhD application, not other Stanford graduate routes.
exceptions: GSB may consider deferral only for rare and extraordinary circumstances, such as compulsory military service.

facts.value: MD financial aid requires an application each academic year after admission offer; no application is reviewed before acceptance. U.S. citizens/permanent residents are considered for need-based Stanford grants and loans and federal loans; international students cannot receive Direct Loans but may apply for Stanford need-based grants/loans. All applicants complete CSS Profile, Stanford supplemental aid application and parent tax records; U.S. citizens/permanent residents also complete FAFSA. Parent finances are generally considered regardless of age; absolute estrangement waiver requires third-party evidence. Institutional aid is need-based, not merit-based. Outside scholarships, MedScholars and RA/TA have separate applications. MSTP and KHS students typically do not apply for regular aid.
conditions: Aid application is annual; required parent information and tax documents apply with limited documented exceptions.
exceptions: International students are ineligible for Direct Loans but can be considered for Stanford institutional need-based aid.

facts.value: External MSTP uses the same AMCAS, Stanford supplemental application and policies as MD. Applicants are first reviewed for MSTP; applicants not selected for MSTP interview are routed to MD Admissions. MSTP admission requires MD acceptance. Research experience is central, with three to six AMCAS letters and research mentor letters desired. Applicants matriculated in another institution MD or PhD program cannot apply; Stanford does not accept transfer applicants. All prospective students may apply, but MSTP stipend and tuition support are limited to U.S. citizens and permanent residents. International students may apply to MSTP only with Knight-Hennessy; otherwise MD and departmental PhD admissions are separate, and any PhD department funding is independently determined.
conditions: Combined degree admission is contingent on MD acceptance.
MSTP-funded places are citizenship-restricted.
exceptions: International applicants may pursue separate MD and department PhD paths; this is not MSTP-funded admission.

facts.value: U.S. citizens and permanent residents admitted to MSPA may be eligible for financial aid. Federal applicants meeting requirements are considered for Stafford and/or Grad PLUS loans; program funds are limited. NHSC and California underserved-area programs offer eligible loan repayment or scholarships. Yellow Ribbon contribution listed for MSPA is USD 13,500 in 2025-26 only. Financial aid is separate from admissions and full-time study strongly discourages employment.
conditions: Program support is limited; federal aid requires meeting Stanford deadlines/requirements.
exceptions: Yellow Ribbon figure is historical 2025-26, not confirmed for 2026-27.

original_scope.cycle: 2025-26 Yellow Ribbon amount; aid eligibility page checked 2026-10-02

facts.value: Stanford Law says it provides no scholarship or stipend funding to LLM students. SPILS funding exists only to an extremely limited degree. Admitted JSD students may receive some need-based aid and research/conference funding; no coverage amount or renewal terms are published. KHS is separately applied for; up to three years of funding may be available, with separate timing and eligibility. MLS program funding was not stated on reviewed official pages.
conditions: KHS requires separate application and does not automatically follow degree admission.
JSD support is described as some need-based aid and research/conference funds, with details unpublished.
exceptions: No SLS scholarship/stipend for LLM; extremely limited SPILS support; no amount identified.

facts.value: Stanford's official 2026-27 Law School tuition category is USD 26,593 per quarter; the published rate is by Law School classification and not limited to JD. LLM programs are nine months/three quarters, so the listed tuition rate establishes the applicable quarterly rate, while the standard single-student cost-of-attendance page separately estimates USD 125,124 on-campus or USD 126,216 off-campus. The COA page does not identify which advanced degree cases its living/loan budget covers. MLS requires at least three residency quarters and full Law School tuition; program-specific non-tuition fees or special registration changes should be confirmed.
conditions: USD 26,593 is per quarter and Law School classified; special registration or multiple-career tuition rules can change billing.
Standard COA totals are published school-wide but are not explicitly assigned to LLM/JSM/JSD/MLS budgets.
Non-tuition fees, insurance and household costs are separate from tuition.
exceptions: Do not report the standard single-student COA as a verified complete advanced-degree budget.
MLS residency requirement is at least three quarters; JSD students may enter TGR status under separate academic rules.

facts.value: All candidates must complete an interview before an offer. Interviews are invitation-only, behavioral and may be remote or in-person; an invitation is not an offer. A valid standardized test score must be on file before an interview invitation. Interview window: Round 1 mid-Sep-mid-Nov; Round 2 mid-Jan-mid-Mar; Round 3 mid-Apr-mid-May. Two to three candidates are generally interviewed per available seat. Admission is need-blind; admission decisions precede financial aid review.
conditions: Interview by invitation only and valid test score must be received; all admitted candidates are interviewed.
exceptions: Interview invitation does not guarantee admission.

facts.value: MBA aid is need-based and available to students of any citizenship who demonstrate need. After admission, students complete the Stanford GSB institutional application annually while enrolled. U.S. citizens/permanent residents submit FAFSA, institutional application, two prior years federal returns and most recent pay stub; international students submit institutional application and two years of tax statements from all countries of work. The gap between cost of attendance and expected contribution is covered by fellowships and loans; average class of 2026 fellowship was about USD 50,000/year or USD 100,000 total. Fellowships are need-based gifts. Financial aid application is separate and admissions is need-blind.
conditions: Need analysis expects student/spouse contribution; consumer debt is excluded.
Aid application and supporting tax materials are renewed annually.
exceptions: Need-based funding applies regardless of citizenship; federal loan eligibility differs by status.

facts.value: JD requires 111 units over no less than three academic years. LLM requires 35-45 approved quarter units, three quarters in residence, at least 26 Law units and full tuition; residence is at least 9 enrolled units and 8 passed units each quarter, with work limited to 20 hours weekly; LLM is a full nine-month academic year. JSM requires 35 units, with thesis and public presentation, and is expected to finish in one academic year (two consecutive years maximum). MLS requires 37 units, three residency quarters, and is expected to finish in one academic year (two consecutive years maximum). JSD requires 44 residency units, including one academic year in residence, and independent dissertation research; award duration beyond minimum residency is not specified.
conditions: These are academic completion requirements, not minimum duration guarantees except where stated.
Law residency requires full tuition and unit completion each quarter.
exceptions: JSD requires 44 residency units but only one academic year in residence under University minimum; actual completion time depends on dissertation/candidacy.

facts.value: Traditional Stanford MD is a four-year clinical degree. The Discovery Curriculum permits students to take pre-clerkship curriculum at full pace over two years or request to spread it over three years, which can extend the MD path to five years. Combined MD-PhD MSTP averages 7.5 years; students generally take six or eight years depending on research and commonly finish PhD requirements one or two years before final clinical rotations. The PA MS is nine quarters (captured separately).
conditions: MSTP completion length varies with individual research; MD pre-clerkship split option is an approved pathway.

facts.value: A qualifying bachelor degree must be completed by July 1 of the year of matriculation. Accepted: a bachelor from a regionally accredited US or Canadian institution (three-year Quebec; four-year other Canadian provinces), or a US graduate degree plus the equivalent undergraduate degree. Online bachelor programs, foreign-only degrees, WES substitution, and waivers are not accepted.

Current Stanford central loan policy says graduate students who have not borrowed for the current degree program before July 1, 2026 are not eligible for new Grad PLUS loans. The MSPA program page checked 2026-10-03 still lists Stafford and/or Grad PLUS; for new August 2027 entrants the two official pages conflict, so Grad PLUS availability must not be represented as generally available.

MD applicants may use AI for brainstorming, organizing their own ideas, identifying clarity issues, and light grammar/spelling edits preserving their voice. AI may not generate substantive responses or frameworks, substantially rewrite/paraphrase essays, or generate reflections, motivations, lessons or conclusions.

Stanford Law advanced applicants must submit TOEFL iBT (not IELTS under the current Law advanced process). Minimum: 100 for tests before Jan 21, 2026; for tests on/after, overall 5.5 with reading/listening >=5.5 and writing/speaking >=5.0. Native English does not automatically waive; applicants must request a waiver with evidence. Waivers may be granted for >=2 years full-time study or work in English. Law page does not specify a validity period; confirm with admissions if score age matters.
conditions: Law advanced-program English requirements are distinct from central nonprofessional thresholds; the common portal policy does not replace them.

facts.value: MSPA is a nine-quarter program with a summer break, clinical rotations, selected California clinical sites, leadership-track choice, and required thesis. Graduates are prepared for PANCE. Accepted/waitlisted candidates receive email; a nonrefundable $1,000 deposit is due by the response date in the individual offer letter and credited to first-quarter tuition. The official pages do not publish a common 2027 cohort response date or placement rate.
conditions: An individual offer deadline is not a universal response date for every admitted MSPA applicant.

value.majors: One BA and one BS major, with no course overlap; BA and BS in the same discipline cannot be combined.

value.last_quarter_in_residence: Required; an approved petition can waive the final-quarter requirement under the published policy.

value.restricted_exception: Stanford BA graduates may request candidacy for BS, and Stanford BS graduates for BA; departmental recommendation and C-USP academic-progress approval determine conditions.
value.boundary: This is a restricted internal Stanford graduate petition; it does not create ordinary external first-year or transfer admission for an existing bachelor holder.
